# DIOPTRICS

## First Discourse.

### ON LIGHT.

The entire conduct of our lives depends upon our senses, among which sight being the most universal and the most noble, there is no doubt that those inventions which serve to increase its power are among the most useful that could exist. And it is difficult to find any invention that increases it more than that of these marvelous <term>telescopes</term> <note>original: "lunettes". In the early 17th century, this term was used for both spectacles and the newly invented refracting telescope. Given the context of "new stars," Descartes specifically refers to the spyglass or telescope.</note> which, having been in use for only a short time, have already revealed to us new stars in the heavens, and other new objects upon the earth, in greater number than those we had seen there before: so that, carrying our sight much further than the imagination of our forefathers was accustomed to go, they seem to have opened the way for us to reach a knowledge of <term>Nature</term> <note>Descartes treats Nature as a system to be decoded through observation and mathematics.</note> much greater and more perfect than they ever possessed. But, to the shame of our sciences, this invention, so useful and so admirable, was not first—

ŒUVRES. I.

->### WORKS OF DESCARTES.<-

only discovered through experience and luck. About thirty years ago, a man named Jacob Metius\*, of the city of Alkmaar in Holland—a man who had never studied, although he had a father and a brother who were mathematicians by profession—took particular pleasure in making mirrors and burning glasses <term>burning glasses: magnifying lenses used to concentrate sunlight to start a fire</term>. He even composed them in winter using ice, as experience has shown can be done. Having on this occasion several glasses of various shapes, he happened by luck to look through two: one which was a little thicker in the middle than at the edges, and the other, on the contrary, much thicker at the edges than in the middle. He placed them so fortunately at the two ends of a tube that the first of the telescopes <note>original: "lunettes"; in this period, the term referred to spyglasses or early telescopes</note> of which we speak was composed. And it is only upon this model that all others seen since have been made, without anyone yet, that I know of, having sufficiently determined the shapes that these glasses must have. For, although there have since been many fine minds who have greatly cultivated this matter, and have found because of it several things in Optics <note>Optics: the branch of science concerned with the properties of light and vision</note> which are worth more than what the ancients had left us, nevertheless—because inventions that are somewhat difficult do not reach their final degree of perfection at the first stroke—there still remain enough difficulties in this one to give me cause to write about it. And since the execution of the things I shall say must depend on the industry of artisans, who ordinarily have not studied, I shall try to make myself...

<summary>Descartes describes the accidental invention of the telescope by Jacob Metius in Holland and explains that despite improvements in optics, the mathematical perfection of lens shapes has not yet been achieved.</summary>

# DIOPTRICS. — DISCOURSE I.

[Page 83]

...intelligible to everyone, and to omit nothing, nor suppose that one must have learned from other sciences <note>Descartes is deliberately avoiding the complex "Scholastic" jargon of medieval universities to make his science accessible to any person using their "natural reason."</note>. That is why I will begin with the explanation of light and its rays; then, having made a brief description of the parts of the eye, I will say specifically in what way vision is performed; and afterwards, having noted all the things that are capable of making it more perfect, I will teach how they can be added by the inventions <term>inventions: here meaning optical instruments, such as the telescope and specialized lenses</term> that I will describe.

Now, having here no other occasion to speak of light except to explain how its rays enter the eye, and how they can be diverted by the various bodies they encounter, there is no need for me to undertake to say in truth what its nature is. I believe it will suffice if I use two or three comparisons <note>Descartes famously uses analogies—like a blind man's cane or grapes in a vat—to explain the physical behavior of light without needing to define its "essence."</note>, which help to conceive it in the way that seems to me most convenient to explain all those of its properties that experience <note>In the 17th century, "experience" often referred to what we now call "experimentation" or systematic observation.</note> makes us know, and to deduce afterwards all the others that cannot be so easily observed. In this, I am imitating the Astronomers, who, although their suppositions <note>original: "suppositions," meaning hypotheses or mathematical models</note> are almost all false or uncertain, nevertheless, because they relate to various observations they have made, do not fail to draw from them several consequences that are very true and very certain.

It has surely happened to you sometimes, while walking at night without a torch through somewhat difficult places, that you needed to use a stick to guide yourself; and you were then able to notice...

<summary>In this opening to his treatise on optics, Descartes outlines his plan to explain light and vision using simple analogies rather than abstract philosophy, aiming to make the science of optical instruments accessible to all.</summary>

# WORKS OF DESCARTES. 3-4.

imagine that you felt, by means of this stick, the various objects that you encountered around you, and even that you could distinguish whether there were trees, or stones, or sand, or water, or grass, or mud, or anything similar. It is true that this kind of sensation <note>The original French word is 'sentiment,' which in the 17th century referred to any sensory perception or feeling.</note> is a bit confused and obscure in those who have not had long practice with it; but consider it in those who, having been born blind, have used it all their lives, and you will find it so perfect and so exact that one could almost say they see with their hands, or that their stick is the organ of some sixth sense, given to them in the absence of sight. And to draw a comparison from this, I wish for you to think of light, in those bodies we call luminous, as being nothing other than a certain movement, or a very prompt and lively <term>action</term> <note>Descartes uses 'action' here to describe a mechanical impulse or pressure exerted through a medium.</note>, which passes toward our eyes through the medium of the air and other transparent bodies, in the same way that the movement or the resistance of the bodies encountered by this blind man passes toward his hand through the medium of his stick. This will prevent you from initially finding it strange that this light can extend its rays in an instant from the sun all the way to us; for you know that the action with which one moves one end of a stick must thus pass in an instant to the other end, and that it would pass in the same way even if there were more distance than there is from the earth to the heavens. Nor will you find it strange that by its means we can see all sorts of colors; and even

<summary>Descartes explains the nature of light by comparing it to a blind person's stick, arguing that light is a mechanical impulse transmitted instantaneously through a medium. This analogy helps the reader understand how we perceive distant objects like the sun through the physical 'action' of light.</summary>
<keywords>René Descartes, optics, blind man's stick, nature of light, instantaneous transmission, sensory perception, mechanical philosophy, 17th-century science</keywords>

### ->DIOPTRICS. — DISCOURSE I.<-

<page-num>85</page-num>

<sig>4-5.</sig>

You will perhaps believe that these colors are nothing other, in the bodies we call "colored," than the different ways in which those bodies receive and send light back against our eyes. You might think this if you consider that the differences a blind man notices between trees, stones, water, and similar things, through the medium of his stick, do not seem any less to him than the differences between red, yellow, green, and all the other colors seem to us. And yet, these differences are nothing else, in all these bodies, than the different ways of moving, or resisting the movements of, that stick. 

Consequently, you will have occasion to judge that it is not necessary to suppose that anything material passes from the objects to our eyes to make us see colors and light, nor even that there is anything in these objects that is similar to the ideas or the sensations we have of them. In the same way, nothing issues from the bodies a blind man feels that must pass along his stick to his hand; the resistance or movement of these bodies—which is the only cause of the sensations he has of them—is nothing like the ideas he conceives of them. 

And by this means, your mind will be delivered from all those little images flitting through the air, called <term>intentional species</term> <note>original: "especes intentionelles." In medieval philosophy, these were thought to be "likenesses" or "forms" that objects shed and sent through the air to the senses. Descartes is arguing against this outdated idea.</note>, which so tire the imagination of the Philosophers. You may even easily decide the question debated among them concerning the place from which the action that causes the sensation of sight originates: for, just as our blind man can feel the bodies that are around him, not only...

<summary>Descartes uses the analogy of a blind man’s stick to argue that light and color are not material substances traveling to the eye, but rather mechanical movements, debunking the medieval concept of "intentional species."</summary>
<keywords>Descartes, Dioptrics, optics, color theory, blind man analogy, intentional species, mechanical philosophy, sensation vs reality</keywords>

...only by the <term>action</term><note>In Cartesian physics, "action" refers to a mechanical power or a tendency to move, similar to pressure.</note> of these bodies when they move against his stick, but also by the action of his hand when they simply resist him; so must it be admitted that the objects of sight can be felt, not only by means of the action which, being in them, tends toward the eyes, but also by means of that which, being in the eyes, tends toward them. However, because this action is nothing other than light, it must be noted that it is only those who can see during the darkness of night, such as cats, in whose eyes this light is found; and that, for the generality of men, they see only by the action that comes from objects: for experience shows us that these objects must be luminous or illuminated to be seen, and not our eyes to see them. But, because there is a great difference between the stick of this blind man and the air or other transparent bodies through the mediation of which we see, I must here make use of yet another comparison.

Imagine a vat at the time of the grape harvest, completely full of half-crushed grapes, and at the bottom of

# PREFACE

The present volume contains:
1. *The Discourse on Method and the Essays*¹, based on the original edition published in 1637 at Leiden by Jan Maire. It was released without the author's name in a <term>quarto|A book size where each sheet of paper is folded twice to create four leaves, or eight pages.</term> format, with two sets of page numbers: 3–78 for the *Discourse* placed at the beginning, and 1–418 for the *Essays*, followed by 31 unnumbered pages containing the Tables of Contents;
2. The Latin version of this work, titled *Samples of Philosophy* <note>original: *Specimina Philosophiæ*</note>. This version was produced by Etienne de Courcelles, a Frenchman living in Amsterdam as a Protestant minister, and was published in Amsterdam by Louis Elzevier in 1644, at the same time as Descartes' *Principles of Philosophy* <note>original: *Principia Philosophiæ*</note>. In this edition, the two works are usually joined together in a single quarto volume, with the *Samples* at the front, consisting of 16 unnumbered pages (title and <term>indices|The plural of index; lists of subjects or names mentioned in the book.</term>) followed by 331 numbered pages. The translator's name does not appear; instead, it features the name of Descartes, who attests (see page 539 below) that he reviewed and corrected the text, acknowledging it as a second edition, at least in terms of its meaning.
Etienne de Courcelles had left out the last of the three *Essays*, namely the *Geometry*. A Latin version of this also appeared during Descartes' own lifetime: **GEOMETRY**, *published in French by René Descartes in the year 1637; now, however, with notes by Florimond de Beaune, Royal Councilor at the Court of Blois* <note>original: "GEOMETRIA, à Renato Des Cartes anno 1637 Gallicè edita ; nunc autem cum notis Florimondi de Beaune in Curia Blesensi Consiliarii Regii"</note>

---

1. See below for the full title on the <term>phototype|An early method of printing images using a light-sensitive chemical process.</term> reproduction of the original edition's frontispiece.

# PREFACE

*...translated into the Latin language, and illustrated with Commentaries, through the labor and study of Frans van Schooten of Leiden, Professor of Mathematics teaching in the Dutch language at the University of Leiden <note>original: "in Latinam linguam versa, et Commentariis illustrata, opera atque studio Francisci à Schooten Leydensis, in Academia Lugduno-Batava Matheseos Professoris Belgicè docentis."</note>. (Leiden. From the workshop of Jan Maire. 1649, in <term>quarto|A book size where each sheet of paper is folded twice to create four leaves, or eight pages.</term> $^1$.)* But this time, although he was on very good terms with Schooten—who should indeed be regarded entirely as his disciple in mathematics—Descartes insisted on leaving him all responsibility for this edition. He expresses himself clearly on this matter in a letter to Mersenne dated April 4, 1648 (*Correspondence*, vol. V, p. 145). It was therefore sufficient for us to point out in the notes the few discrepancies, generally justified, between Schooten's version and the French text; Schooten’s faithfulness is otherwise remarkable, and his Latin style is much clearer and more correct than Descartes seems to have hoped for.

Unfortunately, in this latter respect, the version by Etienne de Courcelles leaves much to be desired. Between the lines in which Descartes confirms its accuracy—which is far too literal and achieved, most often, through the use of strange <term>gallicisms|Idioms or grammatical structures from the French language incorrectly applied to another language, in this case, Latin.</term>—one can clearly read that while he accepts the meaning, as we have said, he does not take responsibility for the style. But, if he did not want to force himself to correct it and leave his mark upon it (which would have cost him more effort than redoing the entire translation himself), he nonetheless certainly made considerable changes: various oversights from the 1637 draft have disappeared; the presentation, in several places, has undergone significant reworking; and additions, of varying importance, are frequent $^2$. All of this is easily recognizable; but the criteria that he—

1. In 1659, Schooten produced a second edition (Amsterdam, Louis and Daniel Elzevier), in which his commentaries are significantly expanded. Augmented by short works by himself as well as by Jan Hudde, Hendrick van Heuraet, Florimond de Beaune, and Johan de Witt, it constitutes, in two volumes, a true <term>corpus|A collection of written texts, especially the entire works of a particular author or a body of writing on a specific subject.</term> of Cartesian geometry at that date. It is this second edition that we have particularly utilized.
2. These additions, at least the most prominent ones, have been indicated in the Latin text within quotation marks.

indicates to distinguish his corrections—namely, the liberties taken in relation to the 1637 text—is clearly insufficient for reliably identifying minor refinements when the author only sought, through the choice of an expression, to clarify his thought a bit better. Under these conditions, it must be said that to ensure whether Descartes, for a specific passage of the *Essays* <note>original: "Essais"; referring to the three essays (Dioptrics, Meteors, and Geometry) published with the Discourse on Method.</note> that one wishes to study deeply, did not have a change of heart before 1644, one must always carefully compare the text of the *Specimina* <note>The Latin translation titled *Specimina Philosophiae*, published in 1644.</note>. We have therefore judged it necessary to provide it in its entirety, in small print; merely indicating the differences in notes on the French text would have led to either excessive minutiae or arbitrary exclusions. Furthermore, the frequency of references to the text of the *Specimina* in philosophical literature made a re-edition of this text desirable.

Regarding the numerous editions of Descartes' first work that followed his death, we did not have to take them into account, as our plan is limited to the reproduction of the original editions. But we provide these in full, from the title to the tables of contents and the <term>privileges|Official legal grants or licenses from the authorities giving a publisher or author the exclusive right to print a work for a specified duration.</term>. Exception was only made for the *errata* <note>original Latin: "errata"; a list of printing errors to be corrected.</note>, which we have naturally corrected in their proper place.

Suitable typographical arrangements have been made to indicate the beginning and end of each page of the original editions and to establish the correspondence between the pages of this edition for the French text and the Latin text$^1$.

It remains for us to say a few words about the principles we followed regarding spelling, particularly for the French text, which alone may be a matter of question. # PREFACE

we would scrupulously follow the editions published during the author's lifetime, the texts of which he himself corrected while they were being printed.

We have in no way strayed from this principle; on the contrary, we consider it increasingly important to restore to Descartes’ writings the orthographic character <note>original: "physionomie orthographique"; referring to the specific spelling and visual appearance of the words as they were written and printed in the 17th century.</note> that characterized them.

In particular, the eccentricities <note>original: "singularités"</note> that the *Discourse on the Method* displayed in this regard could not fail to influence readers, especially those for whom it became a bedside book. This influence, for which it would be easy to provide examples, is revealed—it is true—much more in the handwritten manuscripts <note>original: "autographes"</note> of the period than in printed works. But it persisted for a long time and is by no means historically negligible, which would be sufficient reason for a faithful reproduction of the 1637 volume.

However, to proceed in this matter "as in diplomatic transcription" <note>A "diplomatic" edition is one that transcribes the source exactly as it appears, including all errors and quirks, without editorial intervention.</note> would have been, in Descartes' case, a betrayal all the more blatant because he himself pointed out, regarding the <term>errata|A list of printing errors to be corrected.</term> (see below, p. 514, note), that many mistakes remained to be corrected and that the "distinctions" <note>original: "distinctions"; an archaic term for punctuation marks.</note> often left much to be desired. Jan Maire's edition <note>The original 1637 edition published in Leiden.</note> is, moreover, indisputably very flawed from a typographical standpoint: in particular, the spelling of the same word and, above all, the accentuation are remarkably inconsistent.

The excuse offered by Descartes—namely, that the typesetter did not understand a word of French—means, however, only that the author did not find in Leiden <note>A city in the Netherlands where Descartes lived and published.</note> the valuable assistance usually provided by <term>printing overseers|original: "protes"; the foremen of a printing shop who supervised production.</term> and <term>final proofreaders|original: "tierceurs"; specialist workers who performed the third and final check of the printing proofs.</term> to ensure consistent spelling and to remove grammatical errors; for the more the typesetter was ignorant of French, the more he must have tried to follow the manuscript copy faithfully. It would therefore be necessary to be able to distinguish between genuine printing errors and mistakes in the original manuscript.

Now, while in many cases this distinction is easy to make,

# PREFACE

in many others, one remains in uncertainty. On the other hand, was the manuscript in Descartes' own hand, or had he prepared fair copies <note>original: "expéditions au net"; clean, final versions of a manuscript intended for a printer.</note> for the printer through one or several copyists, who might have introduced, more or less accidentally, forms of their own spelling instead of Descartes'? At least for the *Dioptrics*, the copy was by a specific hand. Indeed, in this treatise, as given in the 1637 edition, the form *ceste* <note>An archaic spelling of "cette" (this/that).</note> predominates, whereas in other parts of the work, this form does not appear at all, and one sees the forms *cette* and *cete* alternating irregularly—the latter alone being authentically Cartesian, as his own handwriting absolutely excludes the other two.

Faced with these difficulties, we could not, however, bring ourselves to overload the bottom of the pages with purely orthographic <note>Relating to spelling and the physical way words are written.</note> variants. This was of no interest, since those we provided in the volumes of the *Correspondence* constitute a body of material more than sufficient for study.

We therefore agreed, first of all, to silently correct obvious printing errors as well as grammatical oversights (singular for plural, feminine for masculine, or vice versa), which likely already tainted the copy. We had no more hesitation regarding inaccuracies of the same kind in the algebraic formulas of the *Geometry*.

Secondly, we have tried to regularize the punctuation according to the sense, while avoiding systematic modernization, which is, moreover, incompatible with the structure of Descartes' sentences. Furthermore, we have conformed the accentuation to the philosopher's well-established usage¹.

---

1. I must add, however, that for ease of reading, I have consistently printed *où* <note>original: "où"; the French word for "where".</note>, as an adverb, in the three *Essays*, whereas Descartes' most frequent usage is to omit the accent, just as he does for the conjunction <note>Descartes often wrote "ou" for both "or" (the conjunction) and "where" (the adverb).</note>. The same applies to *là* <note>original: "là"; the French word for "there".</note>, as an adverb; on the other hand, for *à* <note>original: "à"; the French word for "to".</note>, as a preposition, the omission of the accent never leads to hesitation. # PREFACE

We have, on the contrary, allowed orthographic differences or uncertain forms to remain as a principle, except for removing those anomalies that were too jarring (such as variations within the same page or a single instance appearing against numerous examples of a different form). However, we have corrected everything that seemed to us, with a fair degree of probability, to be the result of either printing errors, *slips of the pen* <note>original: "lapsus calami"; a Latin term for an accidental error made while writing.</note>, or finally, alterations caused by the copyists employed by Descartes.

In summary, whenever we were in doubt as to whether there had been a conscious departure from standard usage on Descartes' part, or simply an indifference between two forms, we refrained from making any correction. We corrected, on the contrary, only when we did not believe the spelling could be what Descartes would have actually intended if he were writing the word with care $^1$.

However, while the principles we have adopted are sufficiently self-justifying, have we always applied them in an irreproachable manner? They leave too large a space for individual judgment to protect us, in every detail, from all criticism. We ourselves, after a final revision of the original text against the already-printed sheets of this edition, feel various scruples regarding a few cases where the evidence did not previously seem at all contestable. For example, *extrordinaire* <note>An archaic spelling of "extraordinaire" (extraordinary).</note> appears—

---

1. The corrected forms are limited to the following, aside from actual printing errors:
1° Use of *y* or *i*. — *Ayt*, *croire*, *aussytost* <note>Archaic spellings for the words "have," "believe," and "immediately."</note>.
2° Diphthongs. — *Ceuillir* and *receuillir* <note>Modern: "cueillir" (to gather/pick).</note> — *neuds* <note>Modern: "nœuds" (knots).</note>. — *transparant* <note>Modern: "transparent."</note>.
3° Plural. — *Nez* (born <note>original: "nés"</note>), *difficultéz*, *esloignez*. The form of plurals ending in *és* is used almost exclusively in the 1637 edition. But at the moment it appeared, Descartes, judging by his *errata* <note>original: "errata"; a Latin term for a list of corrections for errors found in a printed book.</note>, would have specifically preferred the form ending in *ez*. — *Estans* (an isolated form, compared to *estant* <note>The present participle of "to be."</note>). — *Toutefoix* <note>Modern: "toutefois" (however).</note>.
4° The use of *s* for accentuation. — *Voyage*, *batissoit*, *pretast*, *inegale*. — *Despendre* (the Latin etymology requires *dependre* <note>To depend; the editor notes that an 's' was often inserted in Old French to indicate vowel length, even if it wasn't in the original Latin root "dependere."</note>), *étois*. — *Cest*, *cét*, *cestuy* <note>Archaic demonstrative pronouns meaning "this" or "that."</note>.
5° Doubled or silent letters. — *Celluy*, *cella*, *parfaitte*, *esclattant*, *temps*, *trouts*. — *Pieres*, *rons*. <note>Archaic versions of "that," "perfect," "bursting," "time," "holes," "stones," and "round."</note>
6° Use of the *x*. — *Reflection*.

But I must now tell you something about the nature of the senses in general, in order to be able

WORKS OF DESCARTES.
VI.

# OF VISION.
## *Sixth Discourse.*

Now, even though this picture, in passing thus into the interior of our head, always retains something of the resemblance of the objects from which it proceeds, we must not, however, be persuaded—<margin>5</margin>as I have already sufficiently let you understand—that it is by means of this resemblance that it causes us to perceive them, as if there were once again other eyes in our brain with which we could perceive it; but rather, that it is the movements by which this picture is composed which, act- <margin>10</margin>ing immediately against our soul (inasmuch as it is united to our body), are ordained by Nature to make it have such sensations <note>original: "sentimens". In this context, Descartes uses this to mean sensory perceptions or the mental experience of a physical stimulus.</note>. This is what I wish to explain here to you in more detail. All the <margin>15</margin>qualities that we perceive in the objects of sight can be reduced to six principal ones, which are: light, color, position, distance, size, and shape. And first, touching upon light and color, which alone belong pro- <margin>20</margin>perly to the sense of sight, it must be thought that our soul is of such a nature that the force of the movements, which are found in the parts of the brain from which the small filaments of the optic nerves originate, causes it to have the sensation of light; and the quality of these <margin>25</margin>

<summary>Descartes explains that vision is not a matter of the soul "seeing" a literal image inside the brain, but rather the result of physical movements in the brain triggering specific mental sensations. He identifies six primary qualities of visual perception: light, color, position, distance, size, and shape.</summary>

This can be verified by the fact that the moon and <margin>20</margin> the sun, which are among the most distant bodies we can see, and whose diameters are to their distance roughly as one is to one hundred, usually appear to us as being only one or two feet in diameter at most, notwithstanding that we <margin>25</margin> know well enough, by reason, that they are extremely large and extremely distant. For this does not happen to us for lack of being able to conceive of them as larger than we do—seeing as we easily conceive of towers and mountains as much larger—but <margin>30</margin> because, being unable to conceive of them as more distant than one or two hundred feet, it follows from this that their diameter must appear to us as only one or two | <note>the text continues to the next page</note>

For, for example, if, while looking at object X through lens P, one positions one's eye C in the same way it would have to be to see another object which was 20 or 30 paces <margin>5</margin> away from it, and if—having otherwise no knowledge of where this object X is—one judges it to be truly thirty paces away, it will seem more than a million times larger than it is. | There remains only one other way to increase the size of images, which is to make the rays coming from different points of the object cross as far as possible from the back of the eye; but this is, <margin>25</margin> without comparison, the most important and the most significant of all. For it is the only one that can serve for inaccessible objects <note>such as stars or distant landmarks</note> as well as for accessible ones, and its effect has no limits: so that one can, by using it, increase the <margin>30</margin> images more and more up to an indefinite size. <margin>83-84.</margin> ...still left to human art something to add. ...was nothing else, in transparent bodies, than the action or inclination to move of a certain <term>subtle matter</term><note>French: *matiere subtile*. In Descartes’ physics, this refers to a fluid-like substance made of extremely small particles that fills all space and the gaps (pores) between the larger particles of solid matter, acting as the medium for light.</note> which fills their <term>pores</term><note>Small, microscopic channels or gaps within the structure of a material.</note>; and that you should imagine that the pores of each of these <margin>5</margin> transparent bodies are so smooth and so straight that the subtle matter which can enter there flows easily all along, without finding anything there to stop it; but that those of two transparent bodies of different natures, such as those of air and those of glass or crystal, never correspond <margin>10</margin> so perfectly with one another that there are not always several of the parts of the subtle matter which—for example, coming from the air toward the glass—are reflected there, because they strike the solid parts of its surface; and likewise, coming from the <margin>15</margin> glass toward the air, are reflected and return to the inside of this glass, because they strike the solid parts of the surface of this air; for there are also many parts in the air which can be called solid in comparison with this subtle matter. Then, in <margin>20</margin> considering that the solid parts of crystal are even larger than those of glass, and its pores tighter, as is easy to judge from the fact that it is harder and heavier, one may well think that it must cause even stronger reflections, and consequently <margin>25</margin> allow the passage of fewer rays than does either air or glass; though, however, it allows more free passage to those which it does admit, following what has been said above.

<margin>30</margin>motion of the lathe upon a pattern, every small defect in that pattern would leave entire circles marked upon the glass.

### WORKS OF DESCARTES. ###

of Franeker, and Descartes certainly must have entered into relations with him in 1629. On the contrary, he could not have known Jacob Metius personally, who died around 1630; his testimony on the invention of <term>telescopes<note>French: "lunettes d’approche." Literally "glasses for approaching."</note></term> is nonetheless of major importance, especially since, during his first stay in Holland, he would have known, through Isaac Beeckman, who was from Middelburg, the tradition placing the invention in that latter city, if that tradition had already taken shape.

**Page 141, l. 23.** — The original edition reads “*ses nerfs*” (the nerves of the eye); the Latin edition, revised by Descartes, gives *these nerves* <note>original Latin: "hi nervi"</note>, as seen above, l. 18.

**Page 168, l. 3.** — We have corrected the original text which reads: “We will always hear talk of the interior.” In the Latin edition, one reads, in fact, *exterior* <note>original Latin: "exterior"</note>; and, on the other hand, it is indeed the focus called **exterior** here by Descartes, which he commonly designates afterwards as the <term>burning point<note>French: "point bruslant." The focal point where light rays converge, capable of igniting objects.</note></term>, without more precise determination.

**Page 185, l. 17.** — The end of the second book of the <term>Geometry<note>Refers to "La Géométrie," one of the essays published with Descartes' "Discourse on Method" in 1637.</note></term> (pages 352 to 368 of the original edition) is, in fact, devoted to the curves that satisfy the conditions in question. These curves are known under the name of <term>Cartesian ovals<note>A set of curves Descartes discovered while researching the refraction of light.</note></term>, and their invention, which constitutes, in reality, the first solution of an <term>inverse tangent problem<note>A complex mathematical challenge where one must determine a curve based on the properties of its tangents.</note></term>, is one of the most remarkable geometric works of this period.

**Page 218, l. 6.** — It is interesting to compare the <term>Tenth Discourse<note>The final chapter of the "Dioptrics."</note></term> with the letters written by Descartes to Ferrier in 1629 (XI and XIII, *Correspondence*, vol. I, p. 32 and p. 53). The principle of Descartes' machine is always the same: to obtain a piece cut into an <term>hyperbola<note>A specific geometric curve that Descartes believed was the ideal shape for lenses to avoid distortion.</note></term> as a section of a fixed plane by the generator of a cone of revolution. But he returns, in his *Dioptrics*, to the primitive conception abandoned in the letter of October 8, 1629 (see vol. I, p. 33-34), that of a roller whose points will all describe an hyperbola and whose ends will carry the tools used for cutting. However, instead of cutting the glass directly, he proposes, as he did to Ferrier in 1629, to first cut blades and a wheel, which will serve for the glasswork, following a device similar to the one Ferrier indicated (vol. I, p. 47 and p. 59). As for the cutting of the wheel by means of the blades, Descartes no longer speaks, in his *Dioptrics*, of the arrangement recommended in his letter of November 13, 1629 (vol. I, p. 67-68). It seems probable that he was reserving it for himself, and not that he had abandoned the principle.

### 30-31. DISCOURSE ON THE METHOD.

...to slip away beforehand. Not that I imitated the <term>Skeptics</term><note>A school of philosophy, particularly influential in the 17th century, whose followers argued that true knowledge is impossible and that one should suspend judgment on all things.</note> for that reason, who doubt only for the sake of doubting and pretend to be always irresolute; for, on the contrary, my entire purpose was aimed only at securing myself, and at casting aside the shifting earth and the sand in order to find rock or clay. This succeeded for me, it seems to me, well enough, insofar as, in trying to discover the falsehood or uncertainty of the propositions I was examining—not by weak conjectures, but by clear and certain reasonings—I encountered none so doubtful that I did not always draw from it some certain enough conclusion, even if it were only that the proposition contained nothing certain. 

And just as in tearing down an old house, one usually saves the wreckage to serve in building a new one; so, in destroying all those of my opinions which I judged to be poorly founded, I made various observations and acquired several experiences, which have served me since then in establishing more certain ones. 

And furthermore, I continued to exercise myself in the <term>Method</term><note>Descartes refers here to his four specific rules of logic: evidence, analysis, synthesis, and review.</note> I had prescribed for myself; for, besides being careful to conduct all my thoughts generally according to its rules, I reserved for myself from time to time a few hours, which I employed particularly in practicing it on mathematical difficulties, or even also on some others that I could make almost similar to those of mathematics, by detaching them from all the principles of the other sciences, which I did not find firm enough, as you will see I have done in several that are explained in this volume. And so, without living any other...

<summary>Descartes explains that his methodical doubt is not the aimless uncertainty of the Skeptics, but a way to find a solid foundation for knowledge, much like clearing away sand to reach bedrock before building a house.</summary>

## *First Discourse.*

### ON THE NATURE OF EARTHLY BODIES.

<margin>5</margin> <margin>10</margin> <margin>15</margin> <margin>20</margin>
We naturally have more wonder <note>original: "admiration." In the 17th century, "admiration" referred to a sense of astonishment or awe at something unexplained, rather than just high regard.</note> for things that are above us than for those that are at the same level or below us. And although clouds hardly exceed the summits of some mountains, and one even often sees them lower than the steeples of our churches, nevertheless, because we must turn our eyes toward the sky to look at them, we imagine them so high up that even the Poets and Painters make of them the throne of God. They represent Him there, using His own hands to open and close the gates of the winds, to pour dew upon the flowers, and to hurl lightning bolts <note>original: "la foudre." This refers specifically to the destructive power of a lightning strike, often viewed as a divine weapon.</note> upon the rocks. This makes me hope that, if I explain their nature here in such a way that there is no longer cause to marvel at anything seen there or descending from there, it will be easily believed that it is possible, in the same way, to find the causes of everything most wonderful upon the earth.

<summary>In this opening to "The Meteors," Descartes argues that by providing a rational, physical explanation for atmospheric phenomena—often attributed to divine action—he can demonstrate that all earthly wonders are governed by discoverable natural laws.</summary>

<header>158-159. THE METEORS. — DISCOURSE I.</header>

It is true that, since the knowledge of these things depends on the general principles of Nature, which have not yet, to my knowledge, been well explained, I shall need to
<margin>5</margin>make use, at the beginning, of some suppositions <note>Descartes uses "suppositions" here as hypotheses or foundational assumptions that he intends to prove later through his broader system of physics.</note>, just as I did in the *Dioptrics*; but I shall strive to make them so simple and so easy that you will perhaps find no difficulty in believing them, even though I have not demonstrated them at all.

<margin>10</margin>I suppose, firstly, that water, earth, air, and all other such bodies that surround us are composed of many small parts of various shapes and sizes, which are never so well arranged nor so precisely joined together that there do not
<margin>15</margin>remain many intervals around them; and that these intervals are not empty, but filled with that very subtle matter <note>original: "matiere fort subtile." This refers to the Cartesian ether, an extremely fine fluid matter that Descartes believed filled all space, as he famously denied the possibility of a vacuum.</note>, through the medium of which I have said above that the action of light was communicated. Then, specifically, I suppose that the small
<margin>20</margin>parts of which water is composed are long, smooth, and slippery, like small eels <note>Descartes often used everyday mechanical analogies—like eels or bundles of sticks—to explain how microscopic particles behave based solely on their shape.</note>, which, although they join and intertwine, never knot nor hook together in such a way that they cannot easily be separated; and on the
<margin>25</margin>contrary, that almost all those [parts], of the earth as well as even of the air and of most other bodies, have very irregular and uneven shapes; such that they cannot be even slightly intertwined without catching and binding to one another, just
<margin>30</margin>as the various branches of shrubs do when they grow together in a hedge. And when they...

THE METEORS. — DISCOURSE III.

## ON SALT.

### *Third Discourse.*

The saltiness of the sea consists only of those larger parts of its water, which I just said could not <margin>5</margin> be bent like the others by the action of the <term>subtle matter<note>In Descartes' physics, "subtle matter" is an invisible, fluid-like substance composed of extremely small, fast-moving particles that fill all space and transmit forces between larger objects.</note></term>, nor even agitated without the intervention of the smaller ones. For, firstly, if water were not composed of parts, as I just supposed, it would be equally easy or difficult for it to <margin>10</margin> be divided in every way and in every sense, so that it would not enter as easily as it does into bodies that have somewhat wide pores, like lime and sand; or else it would also be able to penetrate in some way into those that have more <margin>15</margin> narrow ones, like glass and metals. Then, if these parts did not have the shape I attributed to them, when they are in the pores of other bodies, they could not be so easily driven out by the mere agitation of the winds or of heat; as <margin>20</margin> is experienced enough with oils or other fatty liquids, whose parts we said have other shapes; for one can almost never make them come out entirely from the bodies where they have once entered. ...always some slight inequality in their size, we should have no difficulty in thinking that the parts of water are not all exactly equal; and particularly that in the sea, which is the <margin>5</margin> reservoir of all waters, some are found to be so large that they cannot be bent like the others by the force that usually moves them. METEORS. — DISCOURSE V.

# ON CLOUDS.

### *Fifth Discourse.*

After having considered how vapors, by expanding, cause the winds, we must see how, by
<margin>5</margin> condensing and contracting, they compose clouds and mists. Specifically, as soon as they become notably less transparent than pure air—if they extend down to the surface of the earth, they are called mists; but if they remain suspended
<margin>10</margin> higher up, they are called clouds. And it is to be noted that what makes them thus become less transparent than pure air is that, when their movement slows down, and their parts are close enough to touch one another, they join and assemble
<margin>15</margin> into various small clumps, which form so many drops of water, or else particles of ice <note>Descartes views the transition from gas (vapor) to liquid or solid as a purely mechanical process where particles simply lose their agitation and stick together.</note>. For, while they remain entirely separated and floating in the air, they can hardly hinder the course of
<margin>20</margin> light; whereas when they are assembled, even though the drops of water or the particles of ice they compose are transparent, nevertheless, because each of their surfaces reflects a part of the rays that strike against them—as was said in the *Dioptrics*<gloss>a</gloss> regarding all transparent bodies—
<margin>25</margin> these surfaces are easily found in sufficient number

---

<summary>In this opening to the Fifth Discourse, Descartes defines the physical difference between mists and clouds based on their altitude and explains that they become visible when individual vapor particles slow down and cluster into drops or ice.</summary>

# ON THE RAINBOW.

## *Eighth Discourse.*

The Rainbow is such a remarkable wonder of nature, and its cause has been so curiously sought after by great minds <note>Descartes refers to "bons esprits" (good spirits/great minds), likely alluding to predecessors like Aristotle or Roger Bacon who also studied the rainbow.</note> throughout history, and so little 
<margin>5</margin> understood, that I could not choose a more appropriate subject to show how, by the method I use <note>Descartes is referring to his philosophical and mathematical method, as *The Meteors* was originally published as an appendix to his *Discourse on the Method*.</note>, one can arrive at knowledge that those whose writings we possess did not have. <margin>10</margin> close to us, whenever there are many drops of water illuminated by the sun, as experience shows in certain fountains, it was easy for me to judge that it proceeds only from the way that the rays of light act against these 
<margin>15</margin> drops, and from there tend toward our eyes. And I see here that the largest angle <term>ONP</term><note>The angle for the primary rainbow, where light reflects once inside the drop.</note> can be 41 degrees 30 minutes, and the smallest <term>SQR</term><note>The angle for the secondary rainbow, where light reflects twice inside the drop.</note> 51 degrees 54 minutes. By adding or subtracting about 17 minutes for the <term>radius</term><note>original: "demi diametre". Descartes is accounting for the fact that the sun is a disk, not a single point of light.</note> of the sun, I have 41 degrees 47 minutes <margin>5</margin> for the largest radius of the interior rainbow, and 51 degrees 37 minutes for the smallest radius of the exterior one. It is true that, when the water is warm, its <term>refraction</term><note>The bending of light as it passes from air into water.</note> is slightly less than when it is cold, which may change this calculation somewhat. <margin>10</margin> However, that could not increase the radius of the interior rainbow by more than one or two degrees at most; and in that case, the radius of the exterior one will be almost twice as much smaller. This is worthy of being noted, because by this, one can demonstrate <margin>15</margin> that the refraction of water can hardly be less or greater than I suppose it to be. For if it were even slightly greater, it would make the radius of the interior rainbow less than 41 degrees, whereas, by common belief, it is given <margin>20</margin> 45 degrees; and if one supposes it small enough to make it truly 45, one will find that the radius of the exterior bow would also be hardly more than 45, whereas it appears to the eye much larger than that of the interior. And <term>Maurolycus</term><note>Francesco Maurolico (1494–1575), an Italian mathematician who made early studies of the rainbow but lacked the law of refraction.</note>, who is, I believe, the first <margin>25</margin> who determined one to be 45 degrees, determines the other to be about 56. This shows how little faith one should place in observations that are not accompanied by true reason. Furthermore, I had no difficulty in discovering why the red is on the <margin>30</margin> outside of the interior rainbow, and why it is on the inside in the exterior one; for the same cause which...

# ON THE COLOR OF CLOUDS, AND OF THE CIRCLES OR CROWNS SOMETIMES SEEN AROUND THE HEAVENLY BODIES.

## *Ninth Discourse.*

<margin>5</margin> After what I have said regarding the nature of colors, I do not believe I have many things to add concerning those seen in the clouds. For, first of all, as for their whiteness and their darkness or blackness, this proceeds only from how <margin>10</margin> they are more or less exposed to the light of the stars <note>original: "astres" — a term Descartes uses for any celestial body, including the sun and moon</note>, or to shadow, both from themselves and from their neighbors. One of which is that the surfaces of transparent bodies <term>transparent bodies: materials like glass, water, or air that allow light to pass through them.</term> reflect a portion of the rays that come toward <margin>15</margin> them, as I have said above<gloss>a. to note, is that even though the action of luminous bodies <term>luminous bodies: sources of light like the sun or stars.</term> is only to push in a straight line the subtle matter <term>subtle matter: the extremely fine, fluid substance that Descartes believed filled all space and transmitted light through pressure, acting as the medium for sight.</term> which touches our eyes, nevertheless the ordinary movement of the small parts of this matter—at least of those which are in the air around us—is to roll in the same way that a ball rolls along the ground, even though it has only been pushed in a straight line. And it is properly those bodies which make them roll in this manner that are called white; such as, undoubtedly, all those that fail to be transparent only because of the multitude of their surfaces, such as foam, crushed glass, snow, and clouds.

Following this, one can understand why the sky, being very pure and clear of all clouds, appears blue, provided one knows that, by itself, it yields no clarity, and that it would appear extremely black if there were no exhalations or vapors <note>Descartes distinguishes between "exhalations" (dry, earthy particles) and "vapors" (moist, watery particles) in his meteorological theory.</note> at all above us; but there are always more or less of them which cause some rays to reflect toward our eyes—that is to say, which push back toward us the small parts of the subtle matter that the sun or other stars <note>original: "autres astres" — a term Descartes uses for any celestial body, including the sun and moon</note> have pushed against them. And when these vapors are in great enough number, the subtle matter, being pushed back toward us by the first ones, encounters others afterward, which cause its small parts to roll and spin before they reach us.

<margin>a. Page 334, line 6, previously.</margin>
This then makes the sky appear white, whereas, if it does not encounter enough of them to cause its parts to spin in this way, it must appear only blue, according to what was said earlier<gloss>a</gloss> regarding the nature of the color blue.

# Notice.

<note>original: "Aduertiſſement"</note>

*Until now I have endeavored to make myself intelligible to everyone; but, regarding this treatise, I fear it can only be read by those who already know what is in the books of Geometry: for, since they contain many truths very well demonstrated, I believed it would be redundant <note>original: "ſuperflus"</note> to repeat them, and yet I did not refrain, for that reason, from making use of them.* <note>Descartes is moving from the descriptive science of "The Meteors" to the rigorous world of "Geometry." Here, he warns the reader that he will not be explaining basic mathematical concepts, but will instead build upon existing knowledge to present his new method.</note>

### BOOK ONE.

->*On problems that can be constructed using only circles and straight lines.*<-

All Problems in Geometry can easily be reduced to such terms that there is no need, afterwards, for anything more than knowing the length of certain straight lines to construct them.

<margin>How arithmetic calculation relates to geometric operations.</margin>
And just as all Arithmetic is composed of only four or five operations, which are: Addition, Subtraction, Multiplication, Division, and the **Extraction of roots**, which can be taken as a kind of Division*; similarly, there is nothing else to do in Geometry, regarding the lines one seeks, to prepare them to be known, than to add other lines to them, or to subtract them; or else, having one...

<summary>In this opening section, Descartes argues that any geometric problem can be solved using the same basic operations as arithmetic—addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and finding square roots.</summary>

<margin>How one can use symbols in Geometry.</margin>
But often there is no need to trace these lines on paper in this way, and it is sufficient to designate them by a few letters, each by a single one. For example, to add the line BD to GH, I name one *a* and the other *b*, and write $a + b$; and $a - b$ to subtract *b* from *a*; and *ab* to multiply one by the other; and $\frac{a}{b}$ to divide *a* by *b*; and $aa$ or $a^2$ to multiply *a* by itself; and $a^3$ to multiply it once more by *a*, and so on to infinity; and $\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ to extract the **square root** <note>original: "racine quarrée"</note> of $a^2 + b^2$; and $\sqrt{C. a^3 - b^3 + abb}$ to extract the cube root of $a^3 - b^3 + abb$, and so on for the others.

<margin>How one must arrive at the Equations that serve to solve problems.</margin>
Thus, wishing to solve some problem, one should first consider it as already done <note>This "analytical" method—assuming the solution exists to see how its parts relate—was a revolutionary shift from the "synthetic" geometry of the ancients.</note>, and give names to all the lines that seem necessary to construct it, as well to those that are unknown as to the others. Then, without considering any difference between these known and unknown lines, one must go through the difficulty according to the order that shows, most naturally of all, in what way they mutually depend on one another, until one has found a way to express the same quantity in two ways: which is called an **Equation** <note>original: "Equation"</note>, for the terms of one of these two ways are equal to those of the other. And one should find as many such Equations as there were lines assumed to be unknown <gloss>*</gloss> <note>These references likely point to contemporary mathematical commentaries or figure diagrams.</note>. I construct the right-angled triangle NLM, whose side LM is equal to *b*, the square root of the known quantity *bb*, and the other side, LN, is $\frac{1}{2}$ *a*, half of the other known quantity that was multiplied by *z*, which I suppose to be the unknown line.

-> $z \infty \frac{1}{2} a + \sqrt{\frac{1}{4} aa + bb}.^\star$ <-

-> $y \infty - \frac{1}{2} a + \sqrt{\frac{1}{4} aa + bb}.^\star$ <-

## BOOK SECOND.

### *On the nature of curved lines.*

<margin>Which curved lines may be accepted in Geometry.</margin>
The ancients <note>Descartes refers here to the classical Greek mathematicians, such as Euclid, Apollonius, and Pappus.</note> rightly observed that among the problems of Geometry, some are <term>plane</term> <note>Problems solvable using only a straightedge and compass.</note>, others are <term>solid</term> <note>Problems requiring the use of conic sections (the parabola, hyperbola, or ellipse).</note>, and others are <term>linear</term> <note>In ancient terminology, these were "curved-line" problems that could not be solved by circles or conics alone; they were often viewed with suspicion.</note>: that is to say, some can be constructed by drawing only straight lines and circles; whereas others cannot be constructed unless one employs at least some conic section; nor, finally, the others, unless one employs some other more complex line. But I am surprised that they did not, besides this, distinguish various degrees among these more complex lines, and I cannot understand why they named them <term>Mechanical</term> <note>The Greeks classified curves like the spiral or the quadratrix as "mechanical" because they were believed to require motions that could not be precisely controlled or defined in pure geometry.</note> rather than Geometrical. For, to say that it was because it is necessary to use some machine to describe them, one would have to reject, for the same reason, circles and straight lines, seeing as they are only described on paper with a compass and a ruler, which can also be called machines. It is also not because

<margin>Demonstration of everything that has just been explained.</margin>
And the demonstrations of all this are evident. For, by composing a space from the quantities I have assigned for the latus rectum and the transverse, and for the segment of the diameter, NL or OP, according to the tenor of the 11th, 12th, and 13th theorems of the 1st book of Apollonius, one will find all the same terms that compose the square of the line, CP or CL, which is <term>applied by order</term> <note>original: "appliquée par ordre." But I must now satisfy what I omitted in the *Dioptrics* <note>original: "Dioptrique"; Descartes' 1637 treatise on optics published alongside this Geometry.</note>, when—after having remarked that there can be lenses of several different figures, which cause rays coming from a single point of an object to assemble all in another point after having passed through them just as well as any other; and that among these lenses, those which are very convex on one side and concave on the other have more power for burning <note>A "burning glass" is a lens used to concentrate sunlight into a small, intense spot to ignite fire.</note> than those which are equally convex on both sides; whereas, on the contrary, these latter are the best for telescopes <note>original: "lunettes"; this term referred to both spectacles and the newly invented refracting telescopes.</note>; I contented myself with explaining those which I believed to be the best for practical use, assuming the difficulty that craftsmen might have in cutting them. Therefore, so that nothing remains to be desired concerning the theory of this science, I must still explain here the figure of lenses which, having one of their surfaces as convex or concave as one wishes, still cause all the rays, which come towards them from the same point or are parallel, to assemble afterwards in the same point; and also the figure of lenses that do the same while being equally convex on both sides, or else with the convexity of one of their surfaces having a given ratio to that of the other.

<margin>How one can apply what has been said here regarding curved lines described on a flat surface to those described in a space having three dimensions.</margin>
For the rest, I have spoken, in all this, only of curved lines that can be described on a flat surface; but it is easy to relate what I have said to all those that one could imagine being formed by the regular movement of the points of some body in a space that has <term>three dimensions: the spatial world of length, width, and depth</term>. Namely, by drawing two <term>perpendiculars: lines meeting at a right angle</term> from each of the points of the curved line one wishes to consider, onto two <term>planes: flat, two-dimensional surfaces</term> that intersect each other at right angles—one perpendicular upon one plane and the other upon the other. For the ends of these perpendiculars describe two other curved lines, one on each of these planes, of which one can, in the manner explained above, determine all the points and relate them to those of the straight line which is common to these two planes: by means of which, the points of the curve that exists in three dimensions are entirely determined. 

Even if one wishes to draw a straight line that cuts this curve at a given point at right angles, it is only necessary to draw two other straight lines in the two planes—one in each—which cut at right angles the two curved lines found there, at the two points where the perpendiculars coming from this given point fall. For, having raised two other planes, one upon each of these straight lines, which cuts at right angles the plane where it is, one will have the intersection of these two... <note>Descartes is describing a method for finding a <term>normal: a line perpendicular to a curve or surface</term> in three-dimensional space by using its two-dimensional projections.</note>

<summary>Descartes transitions from discussing curves on a flat plane to explaining how his geometric methods can be applied to three-dimensional curves by projecting them onto two intersecting planes. He argues that by determining the properties of these two-dimensional "shadows," the properties of the 3D curve are fully defined.</summary>

---

The preceding paragraph is, in Descartes' *Geometry*, the only place where he actually addresses a problem concerning three dimensions. However, the solution he indicates is precisely where he errs, and it is singular that none of his contemporaries noticed it. Not only are there an infinity of <term>normals: lines perpendicular to a curve or surface at a given point</term> situated in the same plane at a given point of a <term>skew curve: a curve that does not lie within a single flat plane</term>; but further, the straight line constructed by Descartes can only be a normal in very specific cases. This is easily seen if, instead of a curve, one considers a straight line in space and its <term>projections: the "shadows" or mappings of a 3D object onto 2D surfaces</term> onto two rectangular planes.

The theory of ovals (pp. 424-431 above) will be the subject of a Note in the volume of the *Works* containing posthumous writings.

As for the elegant construction of the normal to the <term>conchoid: a shell-shaped curve defined by a fixed point and a straight line</term> (pp. 423-424), it has recently been the subject of a remarkable <term>divination: a scholarly reconstruction of a lost or implied mathematical method</term> by Mr. Zeuthen (*New Journal of Mathematics* <note>original: "Nyt Tidsskrift for Matematik"</note> by C. Juel and V. Trier, Copenhagen, 1900, pp. 49-58). This normal is the diagonal of a parallelogram whose sides, directed along the <term>radius vector: a line segment connecting the center of the coordinate system to a point on the curve</term> CA and the <term>perpendicular: a line at a 90-degree angle</term> CH to the fixed line BH, are inversely proportional to the velocities of variation (or to the <term>differentials: the mathematical representation of an infinitesimal change in a quantity</term>) of AC and CH. One has, in effect, easily: (AC — EC) CH = EC . AB; from which:

->      *d*.AC / *d*.CH   =   (AC — EC) / CH   =   FG / FC <-

<margin>Which curved lines may be used in the construction of each problem.</margin>
Although all curved lines that can be described by some regular movement should be accepted in Geometry, this does not mean that it is permissible to use the first one encountered indifferently for the construction of each | <note>This mark corresponds to the marginal note regarding the choice of curves.</note> problem; rather, care must be taken to always choose the simplest by which it is possible to solve it. And indeed, it should be noted that, by the simplest, one should not only understand those that can be most easily described, nor those that make the construction or demonstration of the proposed <term>Problem: a mathematical task requiring a construction or solution</term> easier, but principally those which are of the simplest <term>genre: the class or degree of a curve, determined by the degree of the algebraic equation representing it</term> that can serve to determine the quantity being sought.

<margin>On the nature of Equations.</margin>
Now, so that I may here give some rules to avoid both of these two mistakes, I must say something in general about the nature of Equations: that is to say, sums composed of several terms, partly known and partly unknown, of which some are equal to others, or rather, which, considered all together, are equal to nothing <note>Descartes is introducing the standard algebraic practice of setting an equation to zero (e.g., $x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0$).</note>: for this will often be the best way to consider them.

<margin>How many roots there can be in each Equation.</margin>
Know then that in each Equation, as many <term>dimensions: the degree or highest exponent of the unknown quantity (e.g., $x^2$ has two dimensions)</term> as the unknown quantity has, so many different <term>roots: the values that satisfy the equation</term> can there be, that is to say, values of this quantity: for, for example, if one supposes $x$ equal to 2, or else $x - 2$ equal to nothing; and again $x \propto 3$ <note>The symbol $\propto$ was used by Descartes to denote equality ($=$).</note>, or else $x - 3 \propto 0$; by multiplying these two Equations,

-> $x - 2 \propto 0$ & $x - 3 \propto 0$, <-

one by the other, one will have

-> $xx - 5x + 6 \propto 0$ or else $xx \propto 5x - 6$, <-

which is an Equation in which the quantity $x$ is worth 2, and all at once is worth 3. If, again, one makes

<margin>How many true roots there can be in each Equation.</margin>
<margin>5</margin>
One also knows from this how many <term>true roots: positive solutions</term> and how many <term>false roots: negative solutions</term> there can be in each Equation. <margin>How one can increase or decrease the roots of an Equation without knowing them.</margin>
If, without knowing the value of the roots of an Equation, one wishes to increase or decrease them by some known quantity, one need only—in place of the unknown term—substitute another that is greater or smaller by that same quantity, and substitute it everywhere in place of the first. For example, if one wants to increase by 3 the root of this Equation:

->$x^4 + 4x^3 - 19x^2 - 106x - 120 \propto 0$,<-
<note>The symbol $\propto$ was used by Descartes to denote equality ($=$).</note>

one must take $y$ instead of $x$, and consider that this quantity $y$ is larger than $x$ by 3, such that $y - 3$ is equal to $x$. Then, in place of $x^2$, one must put the square of $y - 3$, which is $y^2 - 6y + 9$; and instead of $x^3$, one must put its cube, which is $y^3 - 9y^2 + 27y - 27$; and finally, instead of $x^4$, one must put its <term>fourth power: literally "square of square"</term>, which is $y^4 - 12y^3 + 54y^2 - 108y + 81$. And thus, describing the preceding sum by substituting $y$ everywhere in place of $x$, we have:

->$y^4 - 12y^3 + 54y^2 - 108y + 81$<-

->$- 19y^2 + 114y - 171$<-
->$- 106y + 318$<-

| or rather

<margin>That by increasing the true roots, one decreases the false ones, and vice versa.</margin>

And it should be noted that by decreasing the <term>true roots: positive solutions</term> of an Equation, one decreases the <term>false roots: negative solutions</term> by the same amount; or, on the contrary, by decreasing the true ones, one increases the false ones. Furthermore, if one decreases either the former or the latter by a quantity equal to them, they become <term>null: zero</term>; and if one decreases them by a quantity that exceeds them, those that were true become false, and those that were false become true. 

As seen here: by increasing the true root by 3 (which was 5), each of the false roots was decreased by 3, so that the one that was 4 is now only 1, the one that was 3 is now null, and the one that was 2 has become true and is 1, because $-2 + 3$ makes $+1$. 
<note>Descartes is explaining the result of the calculation from the previous page ($y = x + 3$). In his terminology, "decreasing a false root" means moving its value closer to zero or across zero into positive territory.</note>

<margin>How one can multiply or divide the roots without knowing them.</margin>

<margin>The reduction of Cubic Equations when the problem is plane.</margin>
Now when, to find the construction of some problem, one arrives at an Equation in which the unknown quantity <margin>10</margin> has three dimensions <term>three dimensions (a cubic equation, where the highest power is $x^3$)</term>, first, if the known quantities <term>known quantities (coefficients)</term> within it contain any fractions <term>fractions (nombres rompus)</term>, they must be reduced to other integers by the multiplication explained earlier. <margin>The method of dividing an Equation by a binomial that contains its root.</margin>
I begin with the last term, and divide $- 64$ by $- 16$, which makes $+ 4$, which I write in the quotient <term>quotient (the result of a division)</term>. Then I multiply $+ 4$ by $+ y^2$, which makes $+ 4y^2$: that is <margin>15</margin> why I write $- 4y^2$ in the sum to be divided: for one must always write the $+$ or $-$ sign as the exact opposite of that produced by the multiplication. Then, joining $- 124y^2$ with $- 4y^2$, I have $- 128y^2$, which I divide again by $- 16$, and I have $+ 8y^2$ to put <margin>20</margin> into the quotient. And by multiplying it by $y^2$, I have $- 8y^4$ to join with the term to be divided, which is also $- 8y^4$; and these two together make $- 16y^4$, which I divide by $- 16$. This makes $+ 1 y^4$ for the quotient, and $- 1 y^6$ to join with $+ 1 y^6$: which makes $0$, and shows <margin>25</margin> that the division is completed. But if any quantity had remained, or if one had not been able to divide without a remainder any of the preceding terms, one would have recognized by that that the division could not be done.

solid (*). <note>This text continues from the previous page, finishing the word "solid." In early modern geometry, a "solid" problem was one that could not be solved with a compass and straightedge alone, but required conic sections.</note> And it is no less a mistake, after that, to try to construct it using only circles and straight lines, than it would be to use conic sections to construct those for which one only needs circles: for in short, everything that demonstrates some ignorance is called a mistake.

The reduction of Equations that have four dimensions, when the Problem is plane; and which ones are solid.

Now, if one has an Equation in which the unknown quantity has four dimensions <term>dimensions (the "degree" or highest power of the unknown variable, such as $x^4$)</term>, one must in the same way—after having removed surds and fractions <note>original: "nombres sours & rompus"; "surds" refers to irrational roots, and "broken numbers" refers to fractions.</note>, if there are any—see if one can find some binomial <term>binomial (a polynomial with two terms, like $x - a$)</term> that divides the whole sum, by forming it from one of the quantities that divide the last term without a fraction. And if one is found, either the known quantity of this binomial is the root sought, or at least, after this division, there remain only three dimensions in the Equation, after which it must be examined again in the same manner. But when no such binomial is found, it is necessary, by increasing or decreasing the value of the root, to remove the second term of the sum, in the manner explained recently; and afterward, to reduce it to another which contains only three dimensions. -> $\frac{tt}{4nnv} - \frac{s}{nn} - \frac{p\sqrt{v}}{nn} + \frac{2my}{nn} - yy$, <-

for the square of CM, which is equal to the square of GH.

->THE END.<-

<summary>In this concluding passage of "La Géométrie," Descartes justifies his brief treatment of complex constructions by explaining that he has provided a universal method for solving equations of any degree. He famously ends by stating he left certain things unsaid so that future mathematicians might have the pleasure of discovering them for themselves.</summary>

### Notice.

Those who visit the Tables of contents <note>original: "Tables des liures"</note> only to choose the subjects they wish to see, and to exempt themselves from the trouble of reading the rest, will derive no satisfaction from this one: for the explanation of the questions marked therein depends almost always so explicitly on what precedes them, and often also on what follows, that one cannot understand them perfectly without reading the entire book with attention. But for those who have already read it, and who know the most general matters it contains well enough, this Table may serve them, both to remind them of the places where the most specific details are discussed—which might have slipped from their memory—and often also to draw their attention to those points they might perhaps have passed over without noticing.

<note>Descartes is cautioning his readers that his "Geometry" is a deductive system. In 17th-century mathematics, proofs were built like a chain; if a reader skips to the middle, they lose the foundational "links" established in the earlier sections.</note>

<term>Notice</term> (French: *Aduertissement*): A common front-matter or back-matter feature in early modern books where the author addresses the reader directly to explain the work's structure.
<term>Tables of contents</term> (French: *Tables des liures*): At this time, indexes and tables of contents were often combined or used interchangeably to help readers navigate dense philosophical and mathematical treatises.
<term>memory</term> (French: *memoire*): Descartes views his writing as a tool to assist human memory, which he believed was limited compared to the pure intellect.

<meta>This page contains the legal printing privileges granted to René Descartes and his publisher, Jan Maire, for the first edition of the "Discourse on the Method" and its accompanying essays. It follows the conclusion of the Table of Contents for "The Geometry."</meta>

By grace and privilege of the Most Christian King <note>A traditional title for the King of France, in this case, Louis XIII.</note>, permission is granted to the Author of the book entitled *Discourse on the Method, etc., plus the Dioptrics, the Meteors, and the Geometry, etc.*, to have it printed in such places as he sees fit, both within and without the kingdom of France. This is granted for a term of ten consecutive years, counting from the day that the printing is completed. No one other than the bookseller he has chosen may print it, or have it printed, in whole or in part, under any pretext or disguise whatever, nor sell or distribute any other edition than that which has been made by his permission, under penalty of a fine of one thousand <term>livres</term> <note>The standard currency of France at the time.</note>, confiscation of all copies, etc. This is more fully declared in the letters issued at Paris on the 4th day of May 1637, signed by the King in his council, Ceberet, and sealed with the great seal of yellow wax on a <term>single tail</term> <note>original: "simple queue." This refers to a method of attaching a seal to a document using a single strip of parchment hanging from the bottom.</note>.

The Author has permitted Jan Maire, merchant bookseller at Leiden, to print the said book and to enjoy the said privilege for the time and under the conditions agreed between them.

->*Finished printing on the 8th day of June 1637.*<-

---

The States General of the United Netherlands <note>The sovereign body of the Dutch Republic.</note> have consented, agreed, and granted, and do hereby consent, agree, and grant to Jan Maire, Bookseller residing within Leiden, that he alone, for the term of nine coming years, within these United Netherlands, associated Provinces and Cities, may print, have printed, publish, and sell a certain book of which the Title is: *Discourse on the Method, etc., plus the Dioptrics, the Meteors, and the Geometry, etc.*. We forbid each and every inhabitant of these lands, within the aforementioned term of nine coming years, to reprint the aforementioned Book in whole or in part, have it reprinted, publish, or sell it, or to bring it from elsewhere into these Lands to be sold or used, without the consent of the aforementioned Jan Maire, upon forfeiture of all the reprinted copies, and in addition a sum of three hundred <term>Carolus guilders</term> <note>A gold or silver coin originally issued under Emperor Charles V.</note>. One-third of this fine shall be applied for the benefit of the Officer who shall bring the legal claim, the second third for the benefit of the Poor, and the remaining third for the benefit of the aforementioned Jan Maire. Done at The Hague on the 20th of December 1636.

**SCHOVENBORCH.**

->By order of the aforementioned Lords<-
->States General,<-

->**CORNELIS MUSCH.**<-
