<meta>This document follows the title page of Descartes' "Specimina Philosophiae." While the title page was for the 1644 Latin edition, this text is the original "Privilege" or royal license granted in 1637 by King Louis XIII for the first French edition of Descartes' works. It establishes the legal protection and authorship of the "Discourse on the Method" and its accompanying essays.</meta>

# ROYAL PRIVILEGE <note>A "Privilege" was a 17th-century precursor to copyright. It was a formal license from the King giving an author or printer the exclusive right to publish a book for a set number of years, protecting them from unauthorized copies.</note>

Louis, by the grace of God King of France and of Navarre, to our beloved and faithful Councilors, the members of our Courts of Parliament, Bailiffs, Seneschals, Provosts, Judges, or their Lieutenants, and all others of our judges and officers whomsoever: To each of them, as it shall pertain, greetings. The invention of the Sciences and the Arts, accompanied by their demonstrations and the means of putting them into execution, being a production of minds that are more excellent than the common sort, has led Princes and States always to receive their inventors with all kinds of rewards, so that, these things being introduced into the places under their rule, they may become more flourishing. Thus, our well-beloved &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Descartes <note>original: "Des Cartes." In many 17th-century documents, the name was written as two words.</note> has shown us that through long study he has encountered and demonstrated several useful and beautiful things, previously unknown in human sciences <term>human sciences: in this period, this phrase referred to the entirety of human knowledge and natural philosophy, rather than the modern social sciences.</term>, and concerning various arts with the means of putting them into execution. All of which things he offers to give to the public, provided he be granted the right to have printed the treatises he has composed and will compose hereafter, whether of theory or of practice, separately and jointly, in such places as he sees fit within or without our Kingdom, and by such persons as he wishes from among our subjects and others, with the customary protections in such cases. We have been humbly petitioned for our necessary letters to this effect. For these reasons, desiring to favor the said Descartes and to make it known that it is to him that the public owes the obligation for his inventions, we have, by these presents, granted, permitted, and we will and it pleases us that the said Descartes may have printed, and shall have printed, all the works he has composed and will compose concerning human sciences, in such number of treatises and volumes as he sees fit, separately and jointly, in such place as he sees fit, within and without our domain, by such persons as he chooses from our subjects or others. And that during the term of ten consecutive years, counting for each volume or treatise from the day it finishes printing, and even before this term begins, no one may print or have printed, in whole or in part, under any pretext or disguise whatever, any of the works of the said Descartes, except those of our subjects or others to whom he has given permission; nor may anyone sell or distribute any other printing than that which has been made with his permission, under penalty of a fine of one thousand livres <note>The "livre" was the currency of France; one thousand livres was a very substantial sum, equivalent to several years' wages for a skilled artisan.</note>, confiscation of all copies, expenses, damages, and interests, with half applicable to the poor and half to the profit of the said Descartes. We command you, and each of you, and enjoin you by these presents, that you ensure the said Descartes fully and peacefully enjoys and uses the contents of these presents, ceasing all troubles and contrary hindrances. And insofar as one might have need of these presents in several places, we will that to the *vidimus* <note>original: "vidimus"; a Latin legal term meaning "we have seen," referring to an officially certified copy of a legal document.</note> and extract of these, duly collated by one of our beloved and faithful Councilors and Secretaries, faith shall be given as to the present original. For such is our pleasure. Given at Paris on the 4th day of May, one thousand six hundred and thirty-seven, and the twenty-seventh year of our reign.

->By the King in his Council<-
->Ceberet<-
->And sealed with the great seal of yellow wax<-
->on a simple parchment tag. <note>This refers to the "simple queue," a method of attaching a seal to a document by slicing a strip of the parchment itself to hang the wax from.</note><-

<summary>This legal document is the official Royal Privilege granted by King Louis XIII to René Descartes in 1637, providing him with a ten-year monopoly on the publication of his works. It acknowledges Descartes' intellectual contributions to the "human sciences" and sets heavy fines for any unauthorized pirating of his treatises.</summary>
<keywords>Louis XIII, René Descartes, Royal Privilege, copyright history, 17th-century law, publishing rights, human sciences, Paris 1637</keywords>

## RENÉ DESCARTES TO HIS READER
### GREETINGS <note>original: "S. D.", short for "Salutem Dicit," a formal Latin greeting wishing the reader health</note>

*These specimens <note>referring to the scientific essays on Dioptrics, Meteors, and Geometry</note>, written by me in French and published seven years ago, were shortly thereafter translated into the Latin language by a friend, and the version was handed to me so that I might, by my own right, change whatever in it pleased me less. This I have done in various places: but perhaps I also overlooked many other things; my changes will be distinguished from the translator's work by the fact that almost everywhere the faithful translator tried to render word for word, whereas I often changed the meanings themselves, and studied everywhere to improve my own sense rather than his words. Farewell!*

# DISCOURSE
# ON THE METHOD
## OF RIGHTLY CONDUCTING ONE'S REASON
## AND SEEKING TRUTH IN THE SCIENCES <note>original Latin title: "Dissertatio de Methodo recte utendi ratione et veritatem in scientiis investigandi"</note><sup>a</sup>

<margin>I. Various considerations regarding the sciences.</margin>
<margin>1</margin>
Good sense <term>bona mens</term> <note>often translated as "good sense" or "the capacity for wisdom"</note> is the most evenly distributed thing among men: for everyone thinks himself so abundantly provided with it that even those who are the most difficult to satisfy in every other matter, and whom nature has never satisfied in any other way, do not usually desire more of it than they already possess. In this, it is unlikely that everyone is mistaken; rather, it provides evidence that the power of judging correctly and of distinguishing the true from the false (which is what we properly call "good sense" or "reason") is by nature equal in all of us. Thus, the diversity of our opinions does not arise from some of us being endowed with a greater share of reason than others, but solely from the fact that we lead our thoughts along different paths and do not consider the same things. For it is not enough to have a good mind; the main thing is to apply it well <term>rectè uti</term>. The greatest souls are capable of the greatest vices as well as the greatest virtues; and those who walk very slowly can advance much further, if they always follow the right path, than those who run and wander from it.

<margin>2</margin>
For my part, I have never presumed my mind to be any more perfect than those of ordinary people; indeed, I have often wished I had as quick a wit, or as clear and distinct an imagination, or as full and responsive a memory as some others. And I know of no other qualities besides these which contribute to the perfection of the mind. As for reason, because it is the only thing that makes us human and distinguishes us from the animals, I am inclined to believe that it exists whole and entire in each of us; and in this I am content to follow the common opinion | of the philosophers, who say that "more" and "less" are only found among the accidents <note>non-essential characteristics</note>, and not among the forms <note>the essential nature</note> of individuals of the same species.

# ON THE METHOD.
<sig>2-4</sig>

...of the philosophers, who say that "more or less" <note>original Latin: "plus & minus," referring to degrees of intensity</note> is found only among accidents, and not among the substantial forms of individuals of the same species. <note>Descartes is referencing a Scholastic philosophical debate: while two people might differ in height or weight (accidents), they do not differ in their basic "essence" or "form" of being human.</note>

But I will not fear to declare that I consider myself exceptionally fortunate to have stumbled upon certain paths of thought from my early years, through which it was not difficult to arrive at the knowledge of certain rules or axioms that constitute the Method. By its help, I trust I can gradually increase my knowledge and finally acquire as much as the limits of my talent and the brevity of life allow me to hope for. For I have already gathered such fruits from it that, although I am accustomed to thinking quite modestly of myself—and while I view the various pursuits of men with a philosophical eye and find hardly any that do not seem vain and useless—yet I cannot help but say that I feel the greatest pleasure from the progress I believe I have already made in the search for truth <term>veritatis indagatione</term>. I have conceived such hope for those things that remain for me to seek, that if among the occupations of men—as mere humans—there is any that is solidly good and serious, I dare to believe it is the very one I have chosen.

<margin>3</margin>
Perhaps, however, I am mistaken, and what I take for gold and gems is nothing but brass <note>original: "orichalcum," a golden-colored copper alloy</note> and glass. I know how prone we are to error when we judge ourselves, and how suspect even the testimony of friends should be when they favor us. But in this little book, I have intended to explain what paths I have followed in seeking the truth, and to portray my whole life as if in a painting <term>tabellâ</term> <note>literally a small tablet or picture</note>; so that everyone may have the opportunity to judge it. Thus, hidden behind the painting, I may hear the free voices of men for my own correction, and add this way of learning to the others I am accustomed to using.

Let no one, therefore, think that I will here deliver some Method that everyone must follow to rightly conduct their reason <term>ratio</term>; for I have decided only to set forth that which I myself have followed. Those who dare to give precepts to others show by that very act that they think themselves wiser than those to whom they prescribe them; and therefore, if they fail in the smallest thing, they are worthy of great blame. Since, however, I promise nothing here but a history or, if you prefer, the narration of a fable <term>fabulæ</term> <note>Descartes uses the word "fable" to suggest that readers can take what they find useful without feeling bound by it as a dogmatic treatise</note>, in which, among some things that will be useful to imitate, there will perhaps be many others that should be avoided; I hope it will be profitable to some without being harmful to anyone, and that everyone will be grateful for my frankness.

From my early youth, I applied my mind to the study of letters; and since I heard from my teachers that by their help one could acquire a certain and evident knowledge <term>cognitio</term> of all that is useful for life...

<summary>Descartes explains that his Method is not a set of universal laws for everyone to follow, but rather a personal "fable" or "history" of his own intellectual journey. He expresses great satisfaction with his progress while remaining humble about the potential for self-delusion.</summary>

I was burning with an incredible desire for learning. But as soon as I completed that course of study <note>original: "studiorum curriculum"</note>—at the end of which it is customary to be admitted into the ranks of the learned—I began to think quite differently. For I noticed I was entangled in so many doubts and errors that I judged all my efforts in learning had profited me in no other way than that I had more and more uncovered my own ignorance.

<margin>4</margin>
Yet, at that time, I was living in one of the most famous schools in all of Europe, where I thought learned men must be found if they existed anywhere on earth. I had been sufficiently steeped in everything with which others there were being imbued. Nor was I content with the sciences we were taught; I had read through whatever books had fallen into my hands that treated subjects more curious and removed from common knowledge <note>Descartes is likely referring to "occult" or "esoteric" sciences which were popular at the time</note>. I also heard the judgments of others about me, and I did not see myself estimated as inferior to any of my fellow students, even though some of them were already being destined to fill the roles of teachers. And finally, I considered this age to be no less flourishing and fertile in good minds than any of the preceding ones. All of this gave me the audacity to judge others by myself, and to believe that there was no science <term>scientiam</term> <note>In this context, "science" refers to any organized body of certain knowledge, not just the natural sciences</note> in the world of the kind I had been led to hope for.

<margin>5</margin>
I did not, however, for that reason neglect all the studies I had pursued in the schools. For I acknowledged that the skill in languages <note>original: "linguarum peritiam," referring primarily to Latin and Greek</note> acquired there is required for understanding the writings of the ancients; that the artful narrations of fables <note>referring to classical mythology</note> polish and stir the intellect; that memorable historical events impel the mind to undertake great things and, when read with prudence, contribute not a little to forming judgment. Finally, I acknowledged that the reading of all good books benefits us in almost the same way as if we were engaged in a familiar conversation with the most excellent minds of all antiquity—who are their authors—and indeed a conversation so well-prepared that they reveal only the best and most select of their thoughts to us. I saw that Eloquence has very great power and contributes much to the ornament of life; that nothing is more pleasant or sweet than Poetry; that many things are found in the Mathematical disciplines that are very acutely invented, which not only delight the curious but also greatly assist in perfecting any works and in lessening the labor of craftsmen; that in the writings treating morals <note>Ethics</note>, many precepts and many very useful exhortations to virtue are contained; that Theology teaches the way to reach heaven; that Philosophy provides the means to discourse with probability on all subjects and excites no small admiration among the more simple; and that Jurisprudence <note>Law</note>, Medicine, and the rest of the sciences heap honors and riches upon those who cultivate them; nor indeed is there any, even among the most...

He provides a balanced critique of various disciplines, acknowledging the utility of history, literature, and mathematics while beginning to question their ultimate foundation.</summary>

<meta>6-8.</meta>

...superstitious and false beliefs. It is not useless to have devoted some effort to these, if only so that we may judge their true value and not be easily deceived by any of them.

But I judged that I had already spent enough time on the study of languages and the reading of ancient books, as well as their histories and fables. For to converse with men of a former age is almost the same as traveling among foreign nations. It is beneficial to know something of the customs of other peoples so that we may judge our own more correctly, and not think that everything different from our ways is ridiculous and irrational—as those who have never left their native soil are wont to do. But those who travel for too long eventually become strangers and foreigners in their own country; and those who investigate too curiously what happened in ancient times usually remain ignorant of what is happening in our own day. Furthermore, fables represent many things as possible which are not at all so, as if they had actually happened; and in this way, they invite us to undertake tasks beyond our strength or to hope for things beyond our station. Even histories themselves, although they may be true, if they do not exaggerate or change the value of things to make them more worth reading, at least omit the lowliest and less illustrious circumstances. Thus it happens that what they narrate never appears exactly as it is, and those who are too eager to model their way of living on those examples are prone to the delusions of the ancient heroes, meditating only on hyperbolic deeds.

I highly valued Eloquence and was inflamed with a no small love of Poetry; but I considered both to be gifts of nature <note>original: "naturæ dona"</note> rather than academic disciplines. Those who are strongest in reason, and who arrange their thoughts in the easiest order so they can be understood clearly and distinctly, can always most aptly persuade others of what they say—even if they used only the barbaric language of the Goths and had never learned any Rhetoric. And those who are born to devise the most ingenious fictions and express them with the greatest ornament and sweetness would be called the best Poets, even if they were ignorant of all the rules of the Poetic Art.

I was especially delighted with mathematical disciplines because of the certainty and evidence of the reasons on which they rest; but I did not yet recognize their principal use. Since they seemed useful only for the mechanical arts, I marveled that nothing more noble had been built upon foundations so firm and solid. On the other hand, I compared the moral writings of the ancient Pagans <note>original: "veterum Ethnicorum"</note> to very proud and magnificent palaces, but built only on sand or mud. They raise the virtues to the heavens with the highest praises, and place them above all other things...

<summary>Descartes critiques the study of history and literature as being like travel—useful for perspective but deceptive if overindulged. He argues that reason and clarity are more important for persuasion than formal rhetoric, and wonders why the absolute certainty of mathematics has only been applied to the mechanical arts rather than to ethics.</summary>

# WORKS OF DESCARTES.

<meta>8-9.</meta>

...rightly contend that virtues should be preferred far above all else; but they do not sufficiently explain what is to be understood by virtue, and often what they grace with such an illustrious name ought rather to be called savagery and insensitivity, or pride, or despair, or even the murder of one’s own kin <note>original: *parricidium*. In this context, Descartes is critiquing the extreme Stoics who characterized their emotional coldness as virtue.</note>.

<margin>7</margin> | I held our theology in high regard, and no less than anyone else did I desire to obtain eternal bliss. But once I accepted as a certain and established fact that the path leading there is no less open to the unlearned than to the learned, and that the truths revealed by God exceed the grasp of human intelligence, I feared I might fall into the crime of rashness <note>original: *temeritatis*</note> if I subjected them to the scrutiny of my own feeble reasoning. It seemed to me that anyone who dared to devote themselves to examining and interpreting these truths would need a special grace from God and would need to be something more than an ordinary man.

I shall say nothing of philosophy, except that, seeing it has been cultivated by the most excellent minds of all ages, and yet there is still nothing in it that is not subject to dispute—and thus nothing that is not doubtful and uncertain—I did not have enough confidence in my own talent to hope that I might find something better there than others had. And when I considered how many different opinions there often are concerning the same matter, each of them defended by learned men, and yet no more than one of them can ever be true, I came to regard almost everything that is offered only as "probable" as being essentially false.

As for the other sciences, since they borrow their principles from philosophy, | I judged that nothing solid or firm could have been built upon such unstable foundations. Neither the fame nor the profit they promise was enough to drive me to their study. For regarding profit, I did not consider myself to be in a position where I was forced by fortune to turn liberal disciplines <term>liberales disciplinas: the "liberal arts" or studies suitable for a free person, as opposed to "illiberal" or vocational trades</term> into a shameful use. As for fame, although I did not profess to despise it entirely like a <margin>8</margin> Cynic <note>The Cynics were ancient Greek philosophers known for their rejection of social status and conventional honors.</note>, I still did not value it highly when it seemed it could only be acquired under a false name—that is, through the knowledge of sciences that are not true. Finally, I judged that I had already tasted enough of all these pursuits—even the most vain and false—to easily guard myself against being deceived by the promises of an alchemist, the predictions of an astrologer, the deceptions of a magician, or the empty boasting of anyone else who wishes to appear to know what they do not.

Therefore, as soon as my age permitted me to leave the oversight of my teachers, I abandoned the study of letters entirely. Having resolved to seek no other knowledge hereafter than that which could be found either in myself or in the vast book of the world, I spent the following years...

# ON THE METHOD.
<page-num>545</page-num>
<header>ON THE METHOD.</header>
<meta>9-11.</meta>

I spent several years in various travels. During that time, by visiting armies, courts, and the halls of foreign Princes, by conversing with men of diverse temperaments and ranks, by gathering various experiences from all sides, and by testing myself in the different turns of fortune, I attended so closely to everything that occurred in life that I seemed to omit nothing from which I might become more learned. Indeed, I judged that much more truth was to be found in those reasonings which individual men use for their own business—and for which they are usually punished shortly after by a bad outcome if they have judged incorrectly—than in those theories which some teacher, sitting idly in a study <note>original: *Musæo*. While literally "museum," in this 17th-century context, it refers to a scholar’s private study or library.</note>, has devised concerning "beings of reason" <term>entia rationis: abstract concepts that exist only in the mind and have no external reality</term> or similar things that do nothing to help in the conduct of life; and from which he expects nothing else, except perhaps that he will gain all the more vain glory the further those theories are removed from truth and common sense; because, naturally, he must have spent that much more wit and industry to make them seem plausible. And I always sought with the greatest zeal the science <margin>9</margin> of distinguishing the true from the false, so that I might see the straight path of life more clearly and follow it with greater security.

I confess, however, that I learned scarcely anything certain as long as I only considered the customs of other men; for I noticed almost as many diversities in them as I had previously noticed in the opinions of Philosophers. And I perceived almost no other fruit from them except this: that when I noted there were many things which, although they seem utterly strange and ridiculous to our customs, are nevertheless approved by common consent among certain other nations, I learned that nothing should be believed too obstinately which only example or custom has persuaded us to accept. And so, gradually, I freed myself from many errors and rendered my mind more fit for recognizing true reasons. But after I had inspected for some time what others were doing in the world and had collected some experiences therefrom, I also proposed to myself one day to seriously examine myself and to inquire with all the force of my wit what might best be done by me. This succeeded for me more happily, I believe, than if I had never departed from my fatherland or from my scholastic studies.

<margin>II. The rules of that Method which the Author investigated.</margin>
I was then in Germany, where the curiosity of seeing that war—which is not yet finished today <note>The Thirty Years' War (1618–1648).</note>—had invited me; and when I was returning toward the camp from the coronation of the Emperor <note>Ferdinand II, crowned in Frankfurt in 1619.</note>, I happened to have to spend the winter in a certain place where, because I had no one with whom I cared to converse and, by some prosperous fate, was free from all cares, I stayed all day alone in a stove-heated room <note>original: *hypocausto*. In the original French, Descartes uses *poêle*. This refers to a small room kept warm by a masonry stove, where he could remain in solitary meditation.</note>, and there I devoted myself most peacefully to various meditations. And among other things, almost the first that came to my mind was to note that those works upon which different craftsmen, not agreeing among themselves, have set their hands, are rarely so per- <margin>10</margin>

<page-num>546</page-num>
<header>WORKS OF DESCARTES. 11-13.</header>

[per]fected than those which were completed by a single person. Thus we see that buildings which were begun and brought to completion by the same Architect are, for the most part, more elegant and better arranged than those which several people, at different times, have built by adding new walls to old ones. So too, those ancient cities which, having been merely small villages at the start, grew into great towns over time, are usually quite disorganized and poorly arranged when compared to those new cities that a planner <term>metator: a surveyor or urban planner who lays out the boundaries of a town</term> has designed freely on a plain. And although, when looking at individual buildings, one often sees as much art and ornament in them as in any others, yet when considering the whole—and how large buildings are joined to small ones, making the streets uneven and curved—they seem to have been arranged by blind and fortuitous chance <note>original: *caeco potiùs & fortuito quodam casu*. Descartes is arguing that "tradition" is often just a collection of accidents, whereas "reason" provides a unified plan.</note> rather than by the will of men using reason. To this we might add that there have always been certain Officials <term>Ædiles: Roman magistrates responsible for public buildings and streets</term> in those cities whose duty it was to ensure that private homes served the public beauty as much as possible; yet we clearly understand how difficult it is to achieve anything truly perfect by merely working upon the labors of others.

In the same way, one may also think that those peoples who, having once been quite barbaric and uncivilized, only attained a state of refinement over a long period of time, and who established no laws except when they were forced to by the inconveniences of crimes and disputes, are usually not as well-governed as those who, from the very moment they first gathered together, observed the constitutions of some wise legislator. Certainly, there is no doubt that the state of true religion, which is governed by laws <margin>11</margin> ordained by God Himself, must be the best-ordered of all, and incomparable to any other. But, to speak rather of human affairs, if the Republic of the Lacedaemonians <note>The Lacedaemonians are the Spartans. Descartes uses them as a classical example of a society governed by a single, rigorous system of law attributed to the legendary lawgiver Lycurgus.</note> was once so very flourishing, I do not think it happened because its individual laws were better than those of other states—for on the contrary, many of them were quite strange and even contrary to good morals—but because they were all established by a single lawgiver, and thus they all agreed with one another and aimed at the same goal.

In the same way, I became convinced that the sciences contained in books—at least those that lack clear demonstrations and are supported only by probable arguments—cannot approach the truth as closely as the simple reasonings that a man of good sense can have regarding the things he encounters, provided he uses only his natural reason <term>ratio naturalis: the innate human capacity to distinguish truth from falsehood without the interference of learned prejudices</term> and is burdened by no prejudice. And I thought this also because we were all children before we were men, and for a long time...

He applies this principle to the "sciences" found in books, suggesting they are less reliable than the unified, natural reason of an individual.</summary>

# ON THE METHOD
<page-num>547</page-num>
<header>WORKS OF DESCARTES. 13-14.</header>

...we were children before we were men, and for a long time we followed the advice of either our desires or our teachers. Because these influences were often at odds with one another, and perhaps neither of them always urged us toward what was best, it is now almost impossible for our judgments to be as pure and as solid as they would have been if we had possessed the full use of our reason from the moment of our birth and had been guided by it alone.

Nevertheless, it would be extreme to tear down all the houses in a city for the sole purpose of rebuilding them in a better style and making the streets more beautiful. Yet, we certainly see that a private owner may have his own house torn down in order to rebuild it; indeed, people are often forced to do this when their houses are <margin>12</margin> decaying with age <note>original: *vetustate iam fatiscentes*</note> or when the foundations are weak and the building is in danger of falling. This example persuaded me that it would not be reasonable for a private individual to think of reforming a state by changing everything from the foundations upward in order to set it right again. Nor, indeed, did I think that the common sciences, or the order of teaching them established in the schools, should be overturned in such a way. 

But as for the opinions I had accepted up until that time, I believed I could do no better than to set out, once and for all, to clear them from my mind entirely, so that I might later replace them with better ones, or perhaps even with the same ones, provided they had been adjusted to the standards of mature reason. I believed that by this method I could guide my life much better than if I built only upon old foundations and relied upon those principles which I had allowed myself to believe in my youth, without ever having examined whether they were true. Although I recognized various difficulties in this, they were not without remedy, and they could not be compared to the difficulties found in reforming public institutions. Great bodies <note>A metaphor for large institutions or states.</note>, once they have been thrown down, are raised up again only with great effort, and once they are shaken, they are held up only with difficulty; their fall is always a heavy one. Furthermore, if there are imperfections in public systems—and the mere fact that they differ so much among various nations proves that many are imperfect—custom has likely made them tolerable. Over time, custom has smoothed away or hidden many flaws that human foresight could not have easily corrected. Finally, these old ways are almost always easier to bear than the change would be. <margin>13</margin> In the same way, we see that royal roads which wind and curve through the mountains eventually become so smooth and convenient from the constant treading of travelers that it is much better to follow them than to try to take a straighter path by climbing over mountain ridges and dropping down over precipices.

<term>Methodus: The "Method" Descartes is developing, based on mathematical certainty.</term>
<term>Ratio: Reason or the light of the mind.</term>
<term>Reformandis: Reforming or reshaping, used here in both a political and intellectual sense.</term>
<term>Scientias: The "Sciences" or bodies of knowledge taught in universities at the time.</term>
<term>Opiniones: Beliefs or views held without the proof of the "Method."</term>
<term>Ædificium: Building; Descartes' favorite metaphor for a system of thought.</term>
<term>Veritas: Truth, the ultimate goal of his inquiry.</term>

He uses the analogy of rebuilding a private house versus a whole city to justify his radical intellectual project.</summary>

# ON THE METHOD
<page-num>548</page-num>
<header>WORKS OF DESCARTES. 14-16.</header>

For this reason, I have the greatest dislike for those fickle and restless men who, though called by neither birth nor fortune to manage public affairs, are nonetheless always contemplating some new reform within them. And if I thought there were even the slightest thing in this writing by which someone might suspect me of such folly, I would never allow it to be published. My thoughts have never reached further than an attempt to reform my own opinions and to build upon a foundation that is entirely my own. And although I am presenting a model of my work here for you because it satisfies me well enough, I do not wish to advise anyone to attempt something similar. Perhaps others, upon whom God has bestowed more excellent talents, will be able to accomplish greater things; but I fear that this very project I have undertaken is so arduous and difficult that it is suited for very few to imitate. Indeed, the mere act of resolving to strip oneself of all the opinions we were once imbued with is not an undertaking for everyone. The greater part of mankind is comprised of two types of people, for neither of whom is such a path suitable. First, there are many who, trusting in their own talents more than is right, are accustomed to judging too hastily; they never take enough time to look around at all the reasons involved, and therefore, if they once dared to call into doubt all commonly accepted opinions and stray from the well-trodden path, they would never easily keep to the track that leads more directly, but would instead wander lost and uncertain for the rest of their lives. The others, however, who comprise almost everyone else,
<margin>14</margin>
possess enough judgment or modesty to realize that there are some in the world who surpass them in wisdom and from whom they can be taught; these people should rather receive the opinions they are to follow from those others, than investigate better ones by their own talent.

As for me, I would undoubtedly have been among this latter group if I had had only one teacher, and if I had never known those diverse opinions which, from time immemorial, have been debated by the most learned men. But I had long ago heard in the schools that nothing can be said so absurdly that it has not already been said by some philosopher <note>original: *nihil tam absurdè dici posse quod non dicatur ab aliquo Philosophorum*; this is a reference to a famous sentiment by the Roman orator Cicero</note>; and I had noted during my travels that not all those whose opinions are very different from our own should be considered barbarians or fools. On the contrary, many of them use their reason just as well as we do, or even better. I had also considered how much the very same man, with the very same mind, might turn out differently if he lived from his earliest years among the French or the Germans, compared to what he would be if he had always been raised among the Chinese or the Americans <note>In the 17th century, "Americans" referred to the Indigenous peoples of the Americas</note>. I considered, too, how even in many matters of little importance, such as the style of the clothes we wear, the very thing that pleased us most ten years ago—and perhaps will please us again ten years from now—currently seems to us ridiculous and foolish...

<meta>16-18.</meta>

...wander; so much so that we are led by example and custom rather than by any certain knowledge. And finally, I noticed that regarding those things whose truth is not very easily investigated, there is nothing less to be believed than a majority of votes; for it is far more likely that a single individual could find them than many. And since I could not choose anyone among the rest whose opinions seemed worthy to be embraced <margin>15</margin> above all others and preferred to everyone else, I was, in a way, forced to use only my own guidance to set the course of my life.

But like those who travel at night and in the dark, I decided to walk with such slow and tentative steps, and to look around so carefully at everything, that even if I did not make much progress, I would at least keep myself safe from falling. Nor did I want to immediately attempt to free myself from those opinions which I had once admitted without any guiding reason; but just as those living in an old house do not tear it down before they have planned the model of the new one to be built in its place; so first I thought about the way I could find something certain, and spent a good deal of time seeking the true <term>Method</term> <note>original: "Methodo"</note> which would lead me to the knowledge of all those things of which my mind was capable.

I had previously studied in the schools, among the branches of <term>Philosophy</term> <note>In the 17th century, "Philosophy" encompassed all branches of knowledge, including what we now call science.</note>, <term>Logic</term>, and among the Mathematical disciplines, Geometric Analysis and <term>Algebra</term>—three arts or sciences which seemed as though they might contribute something to my purpose. But by examining them more diligently, I noticed that, as for Logic, its <term>syllogism</term> <note>A form of reasoning where a conclusion is drawn from two given or assumed propositions (premises).</note> forms and almost all its other precepts serve not so much to investigate what we do not know, as to explain to others what we already know; or even, like the <term>Art of Lull</term> <note>A system developed by Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315) that used revolving wheels of terms to generate answers to any question; Descartes viewed it as mechanical and superficial.</note>, to chatter endlessly and without judgment about things of which we are ignorant. And although it contains many very true and excellent points, they are nevertheless mixed with so many others, either superfluous or even sometimes harmful, that it is often no less difficult to distinguish and separate them than to carve a <term>Diana</term> or a <term>Minerva</term> <note>The Roman goddesses of the hunt and wisdom; Descartes uses this metaphor to describe the difficulty of extracting "pure" truth from the "rough stone" of traditional logic.</note> out of rough marble. As for the <margin>16</margin> Analysis of the ancients and the Algebra of the moderns, they extend only to certain speculations which seemed to be of no use; and furthermore, Analysis is so constantly occupied with the consideration of figures that, while it sharpens and exercises the mind, it tires and harms the faculty of imagination; while Algebra, as it is usually taught, is so confined to certain rules and numerical formulas that it seems to be a confused art which disturbs and obscures the mind, rather than a science by which it is cultivated and made more perceptive. Therefore, I judged that I had to seek some...

# THE WORKS OF DESCARTES
<page-num>550</page-num>
### WORKS OF DESCARTES. 18-19

...another <term>Method</term> <note>original: "Methodum"</note>, in which whatever good existed in those three <note>Descartes is referring to logic, geometry, and algebra, mentioned on the previous page.</note> would be found, while at the same time being free of their flaws. And just as a multitude of laws often provides an excuse for vices rather than a way to prevent them—so that those nations are best governed which have only a few, but which are very strictly observed—so in place of that immense multitude of rules with which Logic is stuffed, I believed that the following four would be enough for me, provided I made a firm and constant resolution never to deviate from them even once in my whole life.

The first was never to accept anything as true unless I recognized it with certainty and evidence to be true; that is, to most carefully avoid all haste and prejudice in making judgments, and to include nothing more in my conclusion than what was so clearly and distinctly apparent to my reason that I could have no way of calling it into doubt.

The second, to divide the difficulties I was to examine into as many parts as would be required to solve them more conveniently.

<margin>17</margin>
The third, to always advance all the thoughts I devoted to seeking truth in a certain order: starting, namely, with the simplest and easiest things to know, so that I might ascend little by little, as if by steps, to the knowledge of more difficult and complex things; even imposing an order in my mind upon those things which do not naturally precede one another.

And the last, both in searching for means and in reviewing the parts of the difficulties, to make such perfect enumerations and such general surveys of everything that I was certain nothing had been omitted by me.

Those long chains of very simple and easy reasons, which <term>Geometers</term> <note>original: "Geometræ"</note> use to reach the demonstrations of the most difficult things, had given me occasion to think that all things which fall within human knowledge follow one another in the same way; and provided only that we do not accept anything false for true, and always observe the order in which one can be deduced from another, there are none so remote that we cannot eventually reach them, nor so hidden that we cannot uncover them. Nor was it difficult for me to recognize where I should begin my investigation. For I already knew that the simplest and easiest things to know were the first of all to be examined; and since I saw that among all those who have sought truth in the sciences so far, only the <term>Mathematicians</term> <note>original: "Mathematicos"</note> were able to find any demonstrations—that is, certain and evident reasons—I understood well enough that they must have been concerned with the easiest subject of all; and that I should therefore examine that very same subject first, even if I expected no other benefit from it...

<summary>Descartes outlines his four fundamental rules of logic—evidence, analysis, synthesis, and enumeration—intended to replace the cumbersome rules of traditional philosophy. He expresses his belief that all human knowledge can be linked together in logical chains similar to those used in mathematical proofs.</summary>

# ON METHOD
<page-num>551</page-num>
### ON METHOD.

...than that I might gradually accustom my mind <term>ingenuity</term> <note>Latin: *ingenium*, referring to natural mental capacity or talent</note> to recognizing the truth and not assenting to false reasons. Nor, indeed, did I attempt for that reason to learn immediately all those particular sciences which are commonly called **Mathematics**; but | because I noticed that, even if they dealt with diverse objects, they all nonetheless agreed in this: that they examine nothing else than certain relations or **proportions** that are found in them; I thought I should consider only these proportions, and indeed in a very general sense, and observed only in those objects which would make knowledge of them easier; and yet I would not so strictly bind them to those objects that I could not easily transfer them to all other things to which they might apply. And then, because I noticed that to recognize what is sought regarding these proportions, sometimes individual ones must be considered separately, and sometimes many must be grasped together and held in memory; I thought it would be best if I simply represented them as straight lines whenever they were to be considered individually; because nothing seemed simpler or more distinctly presented to the imagination <note>Latin: *phantasia*, the faculty of forming mental images</note> and the senses themselves; and I would designate them with certain characters or notes as brief as possible whenever they were only to be remembered and many were to be embraced at once. In this way, I seemed to take whatever was good in *Geometric Analysis* and *Algebra*, correcting the defect of one by the help of the other, and avoiding whatever inconveniences they possessed.

And in truth, I would dare to say that by accurately observing those few precepts I had chosen, I acquired such facility in unraveling all the difficulties with which those two sciences are concerned, that within the two or three months I spent on that study, I not only discovered many questions I had previously judged most difficult, but even finally reached the point where, regarding those very things I was ignorant of, I thought I could determine by what means and how far they could be solved by human ingenuity. Indeed, since I had begun from the simplest and most general things, and thereafter observed the proper order, each truth I discovered served as a rule which | I later used to investigate other, more difficult ones. And lest someone think I am boasting of incredible things here, it must be noted that there is only one truth for each thing, and whoever perceives it clearly knows as much about it as any other person can know. Thus, after a child who has only learned the first rules of *Arithmetic* in school has correctly followed them in adding certain numbers together, he can affirm without boldness that he has found everything regarding the sum sought through that addition that could be found by human ingenuity. For the **Method** which follows the truth...

He argues that once a single truth is discovered through this orderly process, it provides a perfect understanding that cannot be surpassed by any other mind.</summary>

->### WORKS OF DESCARTES. 21-23.<-

...teaches one to follow order and to make accurate enumerations, it does not yield to the certainty of **Arithmetic**.

And this **Method** <note>original: *Methodus*</note> pleased me especially because, through it, I felt certain that I was using my reason <note>original: *ratio*</note> in all things—if not perfectly, at least as well as I possibly could. I felt that by using it, the darkness of my mind <term>ingenuity</term> <note>Latin: *ingenium*, referring to one's natural mental capacity</note> was gradually being dispelled, and it was becoming accustomed to perceiving the truth more distinctly and clearly. Since I had not bound this method to any specific subject matter, I hoped that I would use it no less successfully in resolving the difficulties of other sciences than I had in **Geometry** or **Algebra**. However, I did not for that reason immediately undertake to examine every problem that occurred; for in doing so, I would have strayed from the very order the method prescribes. Rather, I saw that the knowledge of these sciences must depend on certain principles which ought to be sought from **Philosophy**; yet, because I found that in **Philosophy** no sufficiently certain principles had been discovered up to that time, I did not doubt that I must, above all else, think about seeking them out. Furthermore, because I saw that the investigation of such principles was of the greatest importance, and that there was no other task in which haste and the premature adoption of opinions <note>original: *anticipatio opinionum*, often translated as "prejudice"</note> were more diligently to be avoided, I did not think I should attempt it until I had reached a more mature age—for then I was only twenty-three years old—and until I had spent much time preparing my mind for it. This preparation involved both uprooting the erroneous opinions I had previously accepted and collecting various experiments to provide the raw material for my reasonings, as well as refining more and more that **Method** which I had prescribed for myself, so that I might become more firm in its use.

III.
Certain
rules of
**Moral science**,
derived
from this

And finally, just as those who wish to build a new house in the place of the one they inhabit do not merely tear down the old one, gather stones, timber, cement, and other things useful for building, consult an architect, or practice architecture themselves and accurately describe the plan of the house to be made—but also prepare some other place where they can live comfortably in the meantime while the new one is being built—so too, lest I should remain doubtful and anxious regarding the things I had to do (as long as reason persuaded me to be uncertain about those things upon which I had to judge), and so that I might begin from that time to live as happily as possible, I fashioned for myself a provisional **Ethics** <note>original: *Ethicam quandam ad tempus*</note>. This code consisted of only three or four rules, which I will not be reluctant to write down here.

<margin>21</margin> The first was to obey the laws and institutions of my country, and to hold firmly to that religion in which, by the grace of God, I had been instructed from my earliest childhood; and to govern myself in all other matters according to the most moderate opinions...

# ON THE METHOD.

<margin>23-24.</margin>
...moderate, and far removed from every extreme, which were commonly accepted in practice by the most prudent of those with whom I had to live. Since I was already beginning to distrust all those [opinions] to which I had previously been attached, as I intended to examine them anew, I was certain I could do nothing better than to imitate, in the meantime, the actions of the more prudent. And although there may perhaps be some among the **Persians** or **Chinese** <note>Descartes often uses "Persians and Chinese" as examples of distant, sophisticated cultures to show that his rules were based on practical convenience rather than a belief in European cultural superiority.</note> no less prudent than among us, I judged it more useful to follow those with whom I had to live. And to understand correctly what they truly felt was best, I attended to what they did rather than what they said: not only because human morals are so corrupt that very few are willing to say what they think, but also because many are often ignorant of it themselves. For the mental action <note>original: *actio mentis*</note> by which we judge something to be good or evil is one thing, and the action by which we recognize that we have so judged is another; and the one is very often found without the other. Among several opinions equally accepted in practice, I always chose the most moderate—both because these are the easiest to put into effect and usually the best (since every excess <term>nimium</term> <note>Latin for "too much" or "excess"; Descartes follows the Aristotelian idea that virtue lies in the middle path</note> is typically a vice), and also so that if I were to stray, I would at least deviate less from the right path by holding to the middle than if I had chosen one of the extremes when the other should have been followed. And indeed, | among the extreme paths, or (so to speak) among the excesses, I placed
<margin>22</margin>
all those promises by which we deprive ourselves of the liberty | to change our will later. I did not mean that I disapproved of laws which—remedying human frailty and inconstancy—permit us to bind ourselves by a vow to persevere in a good purpose, or laws which compel us to fulfill promises made for the sake of commerce (provided they are not contrary to good morals). But because I saw that nothing in the world remains forever in the same state, and as for myself, I was organizing my life so that I hoped my judgments would daily become better and never worse; I would have thought I was sinning seriously against good sense <note>original: *bonam mentem*</note> if, because I then embraced certain things as good, I had obligated myself to embrace those same things later on, when perhaps they had ceased to be good, or I myself no longer judged them to be so.

The second rule was to be as constant and firm in purpose as possible, and to persevere no less undoubtingly and unhesitatingly in performing those things I had undertaken for very doubtful reasons (or perhaps for none at all), than in those of which I was clearly certain. In this, I would imitate the example of travelers who, if they find themselves lost in the middle of some forest, should not wander in circles, nor even [turn] toward whatever part...

<summary>Descartes outlines the first two rules of his provisional code of ethics: following the moderate customs of his community to remain practical, and being firm in his decisions even when certainties are lacking, much like a traveler walking in a straight line to exit a forest.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Descartes’ discussion of his "provisional morality." Having established his first rule—to obey the laws and customs of his country and hold to moderate opinions—he now details his second and third rules, which focus on decisiveness in action and the mastery of one's own desires.</meta>

### WORKS OF DESCARTES. 24-26.

<margin>23</margin>
...recognize which way they should go, they should not for that reason wander about uncertainly, turning now one way and then another, and much less stop in one place. Instead, they should always proceed as straight as possible in one and the same direction, and not change course later for slight reasons, even if perhaps at the beginning it was a mere whim that made them choose that path over any other. By following this method, even if they do not arrive exactly at the place <column-break/> they intended, they will at least eventually reach somewhere where they will likely be better off than in the middle of a forest. In the same way, because many actions in life do not allow for any delay, it is a very certain truth that when we are unable to discern which is the truly best option, we must follow that which appears most likely to be best. Or certainly, if we find no reason to prefer one over the other, we must still choose one and, once we have embraced that opinion, we must no longer view it as doubtful—at least in regards to our practical behavior <term>praxis</term> <note>original: *praxis*; refers to the practical application of ideas in daily life as opposed to theoretical contemplation.</note>—but as something completely true and certain, because the reasoning that led us to choose it is itself true and certain. This was sufficient to free me from all those anxieties and stings of conscience that usually torment the souls of the weak, who, with a vacillating judgment, often embrace things as good only to later persuade themselves that they are evil.

<margin>24</margin>
The third rule was to always try to conquer myself rather than **Fortune** <note>original: *Fortuna*; in the 17th century, "Fortune" referred to the external circumstances or "luck" that one cannot control.</note>, and to change my own desires rather than the order of the world. More generally, I aimed to firmly persuade myself that nothing is absolutely within our power except our own thoughts. Thus, whatever does not happen—after we have done everything in our power to make it happen—should be counted by us among those things that are simply impossible, or what philosophers call **impossibilities** <term>impossibilia</term>. This alone seemed sufficient to prevent me from desiring anything in the future that I could not obtain, and thus to make me quite happy. For since it is the nature of our will <column-break/> to be drawn only toward those things that our intellect represents as somehow possible, it follows that if we consider all the goods outside of ourselves as equally beyond our reach, we shall feel no more regret at lacking those which seem "due" to us by birth than we do at not being the Kings of **China** or **Mexico**. By adjusting our will most accurately to the necessity of things, just as we do not grieve that our bodies are not as resistant to decay as a diamond <term>adamas</term>, or that we are not equipped with wings to fly like birds, so too we shall not be tormented by the desire for health...

<summary>Descartes outlines two more practical rules for living: being decisive even when certain truth is unavailable (the forest analogy) and focusing solely on controlling one's thoughts rather than external circumstances.</summary>
<keywords>provisional morality, decisiveness, will vs. intellect, Stoicism, Fortune, self-mastery, certainty in action</keywords>

### ON METHOD.
555
<meta>26-28.</meta>

...[nor do we desire health] when we are sick, or liberty when we are held in prison. But I confess that a very long period of practice and frequently repeated meditation is needed to accustom our minds to looking at all things in this way. In this single point, I am convinced, lay the entire secret of those Philosophers who, in earlier times, were able to escape the empire of fortune and, even amidst physical torture and the hardships of poverty, could compete with their own Gods for happiness. <note>Descartes is referring to Stoic philosophers, such as Seneca or Epictetus, who taught that while we cannot control the world, we have absolute power over our own internal judgments and desires.</note> For because they constantly contemplated the limits of the power granted to them by Nature, they became so clearly persuaded that nothing outside of themselves—or rather, nothing except their own thoughts—belonged to them, that they no longer desired anything else. They acquired such absolute command over their thoughts through the habit of this meditation—that is, they so accustomed themselves to governing their desires and other movements of the soul—that they could boast, with some reason, that they alone were rich, alone powerful, alone free, and alone happy. This is because no one else, lacking this Philosophy, can ever have Nature and Fortune so consistently favorable that they might achieve all their wishes as those philosophers did.

<margin>25</margin>
To conclude this ethics of mine, I spent some time weighing the various occupations that people pursue in this life, and I tried to choose the best among them. There is no need for me to recount here what I thought of the others; I will only say that I found nothing that seemed better for me than to continue in the very same undertaking I was then engaged in: that is, to spend my entire life cultivating my reason and searching for truth according to the Method I had prescribed for myself. I had already tasted such fruits of this Method that I did not believe any sweeter or more harmless ones could be gathered in this life. Since I discovered something new every day by its help—things I judged to be unknown to the general public and of some importance—my mind was filled with such delight that no other concerns could affect it. 

Furthermore, the three rules I have just explained would not have seemed sufficiently right to me had I not resolved to persevere in searching for truth through this Method. For since God has granted to each of us some light of reason <note>original: *rationis lumen*; a central concept in Cartesian thought, referring to the natural human capacity to perceive truth clearly and distinctly.</note> to distinguish the true from the false, I would not have thought I should surrender myself, even for a single day, to be ruled entirely by the opinions of others, had I not intended to examine those same opinions with my own intellect as soon as I was properly prepared to do so. Nor would I have been free from the fear of falling into error while following those opinions, had I not hoped that I would miss no opportunity to find better ones, if they existed. Finally, I could not have commanded my desires, nor remained content with the things that are within my power, had I not followed that path through which I was confident I would reach all the knowledge of things of which I was capable.

<summary>Descartes explains that happiness is found in controlling one's thoughts rather than external circumstances, a practice perfected by ancient Stoics. He concludes his "provisional morality" by affirming that his true calling is to spend his life using his Method to cultivate reason and seek truth.</summary>

## ON METHOD.
556
<meta>28-29.</meta>

...and at the same time to the <margin>26</margin> | possession of all true goods to which I might aspire. Since our will is not determined to pursue or flee anything except insofar as the intellect represents it to the will as either good or evil, it is sufficient to always judge correctly in order to act correctly; and by judging as best as we can, we also act as best as we can. This means we can acquire all the virtues along with all other possible goods that can be attained; whoever is confident that they have acquired these things cannot fail to be content and happy.

After I had instructed myself with these rules, and set them aside alongside the matters of faith—which have always held the highest place for me—I did not doubt that I was permitted to clear my mind of all the other beliefs I had previously absorbed. Because I felt I could accomplish this more conveniently by interacting with other people than by staying any longer in that solitude where I had been <note>Descartes is referring to the famous winter of 1619 in Germany where, confined to a stove-heated room, he first conceived of his Method.</note>, I set out to travel again as soon as winter had ended. For the following nine years, I did nothing but wander here and there through the world, striving to be a spectator rather than an actor in the comedies <note>Descartes uses the metaphor of "comedies" to describe the social and political dramas of human life, viewing them with the detached eye of a scientist.</note> that are performed there every day. And as I paid particular attention to what might be called into doubt in every matter, and what might provide us an opportunity for mistaken judgment, I gradually uprooted from my mind all the erroneous opinions that had previously occupied it. | Yet, in doing so, I did not imitate the Skeptics, who doubt only for the sake of doubting and seek nothing beyond uncertainty itself. On the contrary, I was entirely focused on finding something certain. Just as one does when building on sandy soil, I desired to dig deep so that I might finally reach <margin>27</margin> rock or clay. <note>In 17th-century construction, "rock or clay" represented the solid foundation necessary to support a heavy stone structure, preventing it from sinking into the shifting sands of the surface.</note> And this seemed to succeed quite happily for me: for when I attempted to detect the falsity or uncertainty of the propositions I was examining—not by vague and weak conjectures, but by firm and evident arguments—I encountered nothing so doubtful that I could not always draw some certain conclusion from it, even if it was only the fact that the matter contained nothing certain. And just as those who tear down an old house save the materials for use in building a new one, so in casting down my poorly founded opinions, I made various observations and gathered many experiences which were later useful to me in establishing more certain truths. Furthermore, I continued always to practice the Method I had prescribed for myself; I did not only strive to govern all my thoughts generally according to its rules, but I also occasionally set aside a few hours to use it specifically for solving Mathematical problems, or even for questions belonging to other sciences...

<margin>28</margin> | Nevertheless, those nine years passed before I dared to judge definitively on any of those questions usually brought into controversy among scholars, or to seek any principles in *Philosophy* <note>original: "Philosophia"</note> more certain than the common ones. ...so removed from common use that I fear they will not please many; but so that it can be understood whether the foundations of my philosophy are firm enough, I seem in some way compelled to speak of them. I had long ago observed that there are many opinions which—even if they are very doubtful and uncertain—we must follow for the conduct of life just as constantly and fearlessly as if they were certain and proven, as has already been said before. But because I then wished to devote myself entirely to the search for truth, rather than to the management of affairs, I thought I should do exactly the opposite: I ought to reject as clearly false everything in which I could find even the slightest reason for doubt, so that I might experience whether, after those things were rejected, anything remained which I could not possibly doubt. Thus, | because our senses sometimes deceive us, I counted everything I had ever received from them as false. And because I had seen that some people sometimes err even regarding the simplest matters of Geometry and admit <term>paralogisms</term> <note>Paralogisms: Logical fallacies or errors in reasoning, often committed unintentionally.</note>, and knowing that the same thing could happen to me as to anyone else, I rejected as false all those reasons which I had previously held as demonstrations. Finally, because I noted that no thing ever seems true to us while we are awake that cannot also occur to us while we are sleeping—even though such things are then always, or almost always, false—I supposed that none of the things I had ever thought while awake were any more true than the illusions of dreams. <margin>3</margin> But immediately | afterward, I noticed that while I was rejecting everything else as false in this way, I myself, who was thinking this, had to be something. And seeing that the truth of this pronouncement—**I think, therefore I am** <note>original: "Ego cogito, ergo sum"</note>, or "I exist"—was so certain and so evident that no reason for doubting, however enormous, could be imagined by the <term>Skeptics</term> <note>Skeptics: A school of philosophers who argue that certain knowledge is impossible.</note> that would not be overcome by it, I believed I could safely accept it as the first foundation of the Philosophy I was seeking.

Then, carefully examining what I was, and seeing that I could indeed pretend that my body was nothing, and that there was no world at all, nor even any place where I was; but that I could not, for that reason, pretend that I did not exist; on the contrary, from the very fact that I was pretending other things were false, or was thinking anything else at all, it followed clearly that I existed. On the other hand, if I had ceased to | think for even a moment, even if my body and the world and everything else I had ever imagined truly existed, there would be no reason for me to believe that I existed during that time. From this I understood that I was a certain thing or <term>substance</term> <note>Substance: In this context, an independent reality that possesses attributes; here, Descartes identifies the mind as a "thinking substance."</note> whose whole nature or essence consists only in thinking, and which, in order to exist, needs no place, nor depends on any material or bodily thing. So much so that this "I"—that is, the mind, through which alone I am what I am—

[the soul] becomes a thing plainly distinct from the body, and even easier to know than the body; it is such that even if the body did not exist, the soul would not cease to be all that it is.

After this, I inquired what is required in general for a proposition to be known as true and certain; for having already found one that I knew to be so, I thought I could also perceive from that <margin>31</margin> where this | certainty consists. And because I noted that there was nothing at all contained in these words *I think, therefore I am* <note>original Latin: *ego, cogito, ergo sum*</note> which made me certain of their truth, except that I saw very clearly that it is impossible to think without existing, I believed I could take as a general rule that everything which I conceived very clearly and distinctly is true; and that the only difficulty is in correctly noticing what it is that we perceive distinctly.

This being established, I observed that I doubted many things, and consequently that my nature was not entirely perfect; for I understood most evidently that doubting is not an evidence of as much perfection as knowing. And when I further inquired from whom I had learned to think of a nature more perfect than my own, I also understood most clearly that I could not have this [thought] except | from one whose nature was indeed more perfect. As for the thoughts that occurred to me regarding various other things placed outside of me, such as the heavens, the earth, light, heat, and countless other things, I thought I did not need to seek by the same reasoning from whom I had them; for since I found nothing in them that seemed to be placed above me, I could easily believe that if they were true, they depended on my own nature, insofar as it has some perfection; but if they were false, they proceeded from nothing—that is, they were in me for no other reason than because my nature lacked something and was not entirely perfect. But <margin>Note in this place and everywhere in what follows, that the name of <term>Idea</term> <note>Idea: In Cartesian philosophy, an "idea" is any object of thought, representing something to the mind.</note> is taken generally for every thing thought, insofar as it has only a certain objective being in the intellect.</margin> I could not judge the same regarding the thought, or Idea, of a nature that was more perfect than my own. For it was plainly impossible that I had received it from nothing. And because it is no more possible for what is more perfect to proceed <margin>32</margin> from what is less perfect | than it is for something to be made from nothing, I could not have it from myself. And therefore it remained that it had been placed in me by a being whose nature was more perfect—nay, even which contained in itself all the perfections of which I had some Idea; that is, to put it in a word, a being who was God. I added also that, since I recognized some perfections of which I was destitute, it was necessary that there should exist some other <term>being</term> <note>original: *ens*</note> besides me (let me be allowed here, if you please, to use words common in the <term>Schools</term> <note>The Schools: A reference to Scholasticism, the traditional Aristotelian philosophy taught in universities at the time, which Descartes was seeking to move beyond.</note>)—a being, I say, more perfect than I, on whom I depended and from whom I had received whatever was in me. Indeed, in order to know the Nature of God (namely the one whom the reasons just given prove to exist), as far as it can be naturally known by me, I had only to consider all the things of which I found some ideas within myself, whether it was a perfection to possess them; and I was certain that none of those which denoted some imperfection were in Him, and none of the rest were lacking in Him. Thus I saw that neither doubt, nor inconstancy, nor sadness, nor similar things could fall upon God: for I myself would have gladly been without them. <note>Descartes argues that because we consider doubt and sadness to be "imperfections" or weaknesses in ourselves, they cannot exist in a perfect being.</note> Furthermore, I had ideas of many sensible and corporeal <note>Meaning physical things that can be perceived by the senses.</note> things; for although I imagined I was dreaming, and that whatever I either saw or imagined was false, I could not however deny <margin>33</margin> that these ideas | truly existed in my mind. When I then prepared myself to seek other truths, and I considered first of all that object which Geometry deals with, which I conceived as a continuous body, or as a space indefinitely long, wide, and deep, divisible into parts of all sorts of shapes and sizes, and which can be moved or transposed in all ways (for all these things the Geometers suppose to be in that which they examine), I recalled to memory some of their simplest demonstrations. # ON THE METHOD
<page-num>561</page-num>
<sig>71</sig>

<margin>34</margin> [angles] would be equal to two right angles; yet I saw nothing that made me certain that any triangle actually existed in the world. But conversely, when I returned to the Idea of a perfect being that was in me, I immediately understood that existence was contained in it, in the same way that the equality of its three angles to two right angles is contained in the Idea of a triangle, or as the equal distance of all parts of the circumference from the center is contained in the Idea of a circle—or even more evidently. And therefore, it is at least as certain that God, who is that perfect being, exists, as any Geometric demonstration can be.

The entire reason why many persuade themselves that both the existence of God and the nature of the human soul are things very difficult to know, is because they never lead their minds away from the senses, and do not raise themselves above physical things. They are so accustomed to considering nothing except what they can imagine—that is, what they can form a mental image of in their "phantasia" <note>The "phantasia" or imagination was considered by early modern thinkers to be the faculty that processes physical images from the senses, as opposed to the "intellect" which handles abstract logic.</note> as if it were a physical thing—that everything of which no such image can be formed seems to them to be impossible to understand. This is clear enough from the fact that even the Philosophers in the schools <note>Descartes is referring to "Scholasticism," the traditional philosophy taught in universities at the time, which relied heavily on Aristotle.</note> have accepted as an axiom that *nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the senses.* <note>original Latin: "nihil esse in intellectu quod non priùs fuerit in sensu." This was a foundational belief for those who argued all knowledge comes from sensory experience.</note> Yet, it is most certain that the Ideas of God and the rational soul have never been in the senses. It seems to me those who wish to use their faculty of imagination to understand these ideas are doing the same as if they tried to use their eyes to hear sounds or perceive smells—except with the difference that the sense of sight is no less certain for us than smell or hearing; whereas, on the contrary, neither our imagination nor our senses could ever make us certain of anything unless our intellect (or reason) intervened.

<margin>35</margin> Finally, if there are still some who are not sufficiently persuaded by these reasons that God exists and that their souls are things that truly exist apart from the body, I would have them know that all other things they might think they are sure of—such as having a body, or that there are stars, an earth, and similar things—are much more uncertain. For although we have what the Philosophers call "moral certainty" <note>Moral certainty refers to a level of proof that is sufficient for the practical needs of daily life, where it would be considered "insane" to doubt it, even if it isn't mathematically proven.</note> regarding these things, which is so great that no one but a madman would seem to doubt them, yet when it is a question of "Metaphysical certainty," <note>Metaphysical certainty is an absolute, unshakable truth that remains true even under the most extreme, theoretical doubt.</note> no one (unless they lack reason) can deny that there is enough cause for doubt. We must notice that it is possible, while sleeping, to believe in the same way that we have other bodies, see other stars, and another earth, all of which are false. For how do we know that the thoughts which occur in dreams are more false than those we have while awake, since they often seem no less vivid and clear?

<summary>Descartes argues that God's existence is as logically necessary as the laws of geometry and explains that people doubt this only because they rely too much on their physical senses rather than their abstract reason. He introduces the "dream argument" to show that our belief in the physical world is actually less certain than our knowledge of God and the soul.</summary>
