<margin>36</margin>
Let the most outstanding minds inquire as much as they like, I do not believe they can find any reason sufficient to remove this cause for doubt, unless they first suppose the existence of God <note>original: "existentiam Dei"</note>. For the very rule I adopted just now—namely, that all things we conceive clearly and distinctly <note>original: "clarè & distinctè"</note> are true—is certain only because God exists, and because He is a supreme and perfect being, so that whatever reality <note>original: "entis," referring to the "being" or "reality" within an idea</note> is in us must necessarily proceed from Him. From this it follows that our Ideas or notions, being real things that come from God insofar as they are clear and distinct, cannot be anything but true. Therefore, if we often have ideas that contain some falsehood, this only happens because there is something obscure and confused in them; in this respect, they do not proceed from the supreme being but from nothingness. That is to say, they are obscure and confused in us only because we are lacking something, or because we are not entirely perfect. It is manifest that it is no more possible for falsehood or imperfection to proceed from God—insofar as it is an imperfection—than it is for truth or perfection to proceed from nothingness. But if we did not know that all the reality and truth within us proceeds from a supreme and infinite being, then no matter how clear and distinct our Ideas were, we would have no reason to be certain that they were therefore true.

<margin>37</margin>
But after the knowledge of God and of our own mind has made this rule plain to us, we easily understand that the thoughts we have while awake should not be called into doubt because of the errors of dreams. For if someone even while sleeping were to have a very distinct idea—for example, if a Geometer were to discover some new demonstration—his sleep would certainly not prevent it from being true. As for the error most common to our dreams—which consists of representing various objects to us in the same way they are shown by the external senses while we are awake—it does not matter if it gives us reason to distrust such ideas (which we either receive or think we receive from the senses). After all, these senses can often deceive us even while we are awake, as when those suffering from jaundice <note>original: "morbo regio," literally "the royal disease," an old term for jaundice which can cause yellowed vision.</note> see everything tinted with a yellow color, or when the stars or other very distant bodies appear much smaller to us than they actually are. For ultimately, whether we are awake or asleep, we ought to follow the evidence of our reason <note>original: "evidentiam rationis"</note> alone in our judgments. It must be noted here that I am speaking of the evidence of our reason, and not of our imagination or our senses. Thus, for example, although we see the Sun very clearly, we should not judge it to be only the size that our eyes show us; and although we can distinctly imagine the head of a lion—

<note>original vocabulary: existence of God, clear and distinct ideas, reason, dreams, senses, imagination, jaundice, the Sun</note>

### 40-42. ON THE METHOD.

...joined to the body of a goat, one should not conclude from this that a chimera exists in the world. For Reason <note>original: "Ratio"</note> does not dictate to us that those things we see or imagine in this way therefore truly exist. But it clearly dictates to us that all our Ideas <note>original: "Ideas"</note> or notions contain some truth in themselves; for otherwise it would not be possible for God <note>original: "Deus"</note>, who is supremely perfect and truthful, to have placed them in us. And because our reasoning or judgments are never as clear and distinct while we sleep as when we are awake—even if our imaginations are sometimes more vivid and expressive—Reason also dictates to us that since all our thoughts cannot be true (because we are not entirely perfect), those that are most true among them are rather the ones we have while awake, than those occurring to us while sleeping.

<margin>38</margin>
<margin>V. The order of Physical questions investigated by the Author; and specifically the motion of the heart, and the clarification of certain other difficult opinions regarding Medicine; then, what the difference is between our soul and that of the beasts <note>original: "brutorum"</note>.</margin>
I would very gladly proceed here and display the entire chain of truths that I have derived from these first principles; but since for this matter it would now be necessary to deal with various questions contested among the learned—with whom I do not wish to "pull the rope of contention" <note>An idiom meaning to engage in a back-and-forth argument or tug-of-war</note>—I believe it will be better for me to abstain from them, and only say in general what they are, so that the wiser may judge whether it is helpful for the "republic of letters" <term>Republic of Letters: The international community of intellectuals and scholars who shared knowledge through letters and publications.</term> to be more specifically informed about them. I have always remained firm in my purpose of assuming no other principle besides that which I have just used to demonstrate the existence of God and of the soul <note>original: "animæ"</note>, and of accepting nothing as true unless it appeared to me clearer and more certain than the demonstrations of the Geometers had previously seemed. Nevertheless, I dare to say that I have not only found the way to satisfy myself in a short time regarding all the primary questions usually treated in Philosophy; but also that I have observed certain laws <note>original: "leges"</note> so established by God in nature, and of which He has impressed such notions in our minds, that after we have given them enough attention, we cannot doubt that they are accurately observed in everything that exists or happens in the world. Then, considering the sequence of those laws, I seem to have noticed many truths of greater importance than all I had learned before, or even hoped I could learn.

But because I have attempted to explain the chief of these in a particular treatise—which some reasons <note>Descartes is likely referring to the condemnation of Galileo by the Church in 1633, which caused him to suppress his own scientific work, *The World*.</note> prevent me from publishing—I cannot reveal what they are more conveniently than if I briefly recount the summary of that treatise here. My purpose in it was to encompass everything I thought I knew about the nature of material things before I set about writing it. But just as painters, since they cannot equally exhibit all the faces of a solid body on a flat canvas, select one of the primary ones which alone they turn toward the light, while shading the others, | and so far...

...they only allow [the other sides] to be seen insofar as they can be viewed while looking at the primary side. In the same way, fearing that I could not include everything I had in mind within my dissertation, I decided to set forth at length only what I conceived regarding the nature of light. Then, taking that opportunity, I would add something about the 
<margin>39</margin>
Sun and the fixed stars, because light almost entirely | emanates from them; also about the heavens, because they transmit it; about the Planets, Comets, and the Earth, because they reflect it; and specifically about all the bodies that occur on earth, because they are either colored, or transparent, or luminous; and finally about man, because he is the spectator of these things. Furthermore, to cast some shadows over all these subjects and to be able to say more freely what I thought about them, without being bound to either follow or refute the opinions accepted among the learned, I decided to leave this entire World to their disputes. I chose to treat only what would happen in a New World, if God <note>original: "Deus"</note> were now to create, somewhere in imaginary spaces, a sufficient quantity of matter to compose it, and were to agitate the various parts of this matter in different ways and without order, so that he composed from it a Chaos as confused as any the Poets could imagine; and if He thereafter did nothing more than lend His ordinary concurrence <term>concurrence: the theological idea that God must continuously sustain the existence and actions of all created things</term> to nature, and allowed nature to act according to the laws He had established.

Thus, I first described this matter and attempted to depict it in such a way that nothing, in my opinion, is clearer or more intelligible in the world, except for those things just said concerning God and the Soul. For I even explicitly supposed that | there were no such "forms" or "qualities" in this matter as those disputed in the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to Scholasticism, the dominant Aristotelian philosophy of the time, which Descartes was attempting to replace</note>, nor anything in general the knowledge of which is not so natural to our minds that no one could claim to be ignorant of it. 

Furthermore, I showed what the laws of nature were; and assuming no other principle to establish my reasons except the infinite perfection of God, I studied how to demonstrate all those laws about which any doubt might arise. I aimed to prove that even if
<margin>40</margin>
God | had created many worlds, there could be none in which these laws were not accurately observed. Afterward, I showed how the greatest part of the matter in that Chaos, according to these laws, would dispose and arrange itself in such a way as to become similar to our Heavens; how, meanwhile, some of its parts would compose the Earth, others the Planets and Comets, and still others the Sun and fixed stars. And at this point, digressing into a treatise on Light, I explained at length what kind of light that would be which composed the Sun and the stars, and how from there it would traverse the immense spaces of the heavens in a moment of time, and be reflected from the Planets and Comets toward the earth. I also added many things there concerning the substance, position, movements, and all the various stars of those heavens...

I also showed how, since its surface was covered with water and air, the arrangement of the Heavens and the Stars, and especially the Moon, would necessarily cause a flow and ebb <note>original: "fluxum & refluxum"; Descartes is explaining the tides through his theory of celestial pressure</note> in it, similar in all its circumstances to that which is observed in our seas; and furthermore, a certain movement of the water and air from east to west, such as is noticed between the Tropics. I explained how it can induce various colors into different bodies, along with various other qualities; how it melts some things and hardens others; how it can consume almost everything or turn it into ash and smoke; and finally, how from these ashes, by the sole force of its action, it can create glass <note>original: "vitrum"</note>. For since this transmutation of ashes into glass is as admirable as any other that occurs in nature, I chose to take some pleasure in a detailed description of it.

I did not, however, wish to infer from all these things that this World was created in the manner I was proposing. For it is much more likely that God made it from the beginning such as it was destined to be. Nevertheless, it is certain, and a point commonly accepted among Theologians <note>original: "Theologos"</note>, that the action by which He now preserves the world is the same as that by which He once created it. Thus, even if He had given the world no other form than Chaos at the beginning, provided that after establishing the laws of nature He lent His concurrence <term>concurrence: the theological concept that God must continuously "act along with" nature for it to function</term> to it to act as it usually does, one can believe—without doing any injustice to the miracle of creation—that all purely material things could, over time, have become such as we now see them to be. Indeed, their nature is much more easily understood when they are seen arising little by little in this way than when they are only considered as completed and perfect.

But because I did not yet possess enough knowledge of them to treat them with the same method I used for the others—that is, by demonstrating effects through their causes, and showing from what seeds and in what way nature must produce them—I was content to suppose that God formed the body of a man entirely similar to one of our own. I assumed this body was the same in the external shape of its limbs as well as in the internal configuration of its organs, and made from the same matter I had previously described. I also supposed that, at the beginning, God did not place a rational soul <note>original: "animam rationalem"</note> in it, nor anything else to serve as a vegetative or sensitive soul <note>These were traditional Aristotelian terms: the "vegetative soul" was thought to govern growth, and the "sensitive soul" to govern movement and sensation. For when I examined the functions that could consequently exist in this human body, I found all those that can exist in us without our thinking about them—and therefore without the cooperation of the soul, that is, that part of us distinct from the body whose nature (as has been said before) consists solely in thinking. These are the same functions in which animals, which are said to lack reason, can be said to resemble us. However, I could not find any of those functions which, depending on the mind, belong to us alone insofar as we are human. I found these later, after I had supposed that God created a rational soul and joined it to this body in a certain way that I was describing.

<margin>43</margin>

Since this is the first and most general movement observed in animals, it will be easy to judge from it how all the rest should be regarded. And so that there may be less difficulty in perceiving what I am about to say, I advise those who are not versed in anatomy <note>original: "Anatomiâ"</note> that, before they set about reading this, they should have the heart of some large animal that has lungs dissected in their presence (for in all of them it is sufficiently similar to the human heart), and have the two ventricles <term>ventricle: a hollow chamber or cavity within an organ, specifically the heart</term> or cavities that are there shown to them. Descartes notes it is "badly named" because it is structurally an artery but was historically called a vein.</note>, which, having its origin in the heart, is divided into many branches after it leaves, which are then dispersed through the lungs. Second, the ventricle that is on the left side, to which two channels correspond in the same way, being just as large as the preceding ones, if not...

<margin>44</margin> ...more specifically: the **pulmonary vein** <note>original: "arteria venosa"</note>, which is also poorly named, since it is nothing other than a vein that originates in the lungs, where it is divided into many branches. These branches are intertwined with those of the **pulmonary artery** <note>original: "venae arteriosae"</note> and the **windpipe** <note>original: "asperae arteriae"</note>, through which the air we breathe enters; and the **aorta** <note>original: "magna arteria"</note>, which, exiting from the heart, disperses its branches throughout the entire body. I would also wish to have shown to them, with great care, the eleven little membranes <note>Descartes refers to the heart valves as membranes or "pelliculas."</note> which, like so many valves, open and close the four openings or orifices found in these two cavities. Namely:

Three at the entrance of the **vena cava**, where they are positioned in such a way that they can in no way prevent the blood they contain from flowing into the right ventricle of the heart, even though they accurately prevent it from exiting. Three at the entrance of the pulmonary artery, which, arranged in the opposite way, allow the blood contained in that cavity to pass to the lungs, but do not allow the blood in the lungs to return there. And likewise, two others at the orifice of the pulmonary vein, which allow blood to flow from the lungs into the left ventricle of the heart, but block its return. And finally, three at the entrance of the aorta, which allow blood to exit the heart, but prevent it from returning.

There is no need to seek any other cause for the number of these membranes than this: since the orifice of the pulmonary vein is oval-shaped due to its location, it can be conveniently closed by two; whereas the others, being round, can be better blocked by three. Furthermore, I would wish it to be shown to them that the aorta and the pulmonary artery are of a much harder and firmer composition than the pulmonary vein and the vena cava; and that these last two dilate before they enter the heart, forming two pouches there commonly called the **auricles of the heart** <note>original: "auriculae cordis"; today these are known as the atria.</note>, which are composed of flesh similar to the heart itself. There is always much more heat in the heart than in any other part of the body; and finally, this heat is capable of causing any drop of blood that enters its cavities to immediately swell and **expand** <note>original: "dilatetur"</note>, just as happens generally to all liquids when they fall drop by drop into a very hot vessel.

<margin>45</margin> After this, I need say nothing more to explain the movement of the heart, except that when its cavities are not full of blood, blood necessarily flows there—from the vena cava into the right side, and from the pulmonary vein into the left—because these two vessels are always full of blood, and their orifices facing the heart cannot then be closed. But as soon as two drops of blood have entered in this way (one into each cavity), since they are necessarily very large because the openings through which they enter are wide and the vessels from which they come are full of blood, they immediately **rarefy** and expand because of the heat they find there. By this means, it happens that...

...cause the entire heart to swell, and at the same time they push against and close the five valves which are at the entry of the vessels from which they flow, preventing a greater quantity of blood from descending into the heart. As the blood becomes more and more <term>rarefied</term> <note>Descartes believed the heart acted like a boiler where blood expanded (rarefied) due to heat, rather than the heart being a muscle that contracts.</note>, it simultaneously pushes against and opens the six remaining valves located at the orifices of the two other vessels through which the blood exits. In this way, they cause all the branches of the **pulmonary artery** <note>original: "venae arteriosae"</note> and the **aorta** <note>original: "magna arteria"</note> to swell at almost the same moment as the heart. 

Immediately afterward, the heart—as well as these arteries—collapses <note>original: "detumescit"</note>, because the blood that entered has cooled, and those six valves close. Then the five valves of the **vena cava** and the **pulmonary vein** <note>original: "arteriae venosae"</note> open up again, providing a passage | for two more drops of blood, which again cause the heart and arteries to swell just like the previous ones. And because the blood that enters the heart in this way passes through those two **auricles** <note>The upper chambers of the heart, now called atria.</note>, it follows that their movement is the opposite of the heart's movement: when the heart swells, they collapse.

Furthermore, lest those who are ignorant of the power of mathematical demonstrations, and are not practiced in distinguishing true reasons from those that are merely probable, should dare to deny this without a prior examination; I wish to warn them that this motion I have just explained follows as necessarily from the mere arrangement of the organs (which they can see with their own eyes in the heart), and from the heat which can be felt with the fingers, and from the nature of the blood which is known by experience, as the movement of a **clock** follows from the force, position, and shape of the weights and wheels of which it is composed.

<margin>Harvey, *On the Motion of the Heart*.</margin>
| But if it is asked how it happens that the blood in the veins, flowing thus continually <margin>46</margin> into the heart, is not exhausted, and why the arteries do not become too full since all the blood passing through the heart enters them; I need not answer anything other than what has already been written by a certain **English Physician** <note>A reference to William Harvey (1578–1657), who published his discovery of the circulation of the blood in 1628.</note>. To him must be given the credit for having **broken the ice** in this matter; he was the first to teach that there are many tiny passages at the ends of the arteries through which the blood they receive from the heart enters the small branches of the veins, from where it returns again to the heart. Thus, the movement of the blood is nothing other than a perpetual | **circulation**. 

This is very well proven by the common experience of surgeons: by tying a bandage with moderate tightness around an arm above the spot where they open a vein, they cause the blood to burst forth more abundantly than if they had not tied it. Quite the opposite would happen if they tied the arm below—that is, between the hand and the opening—or if they tied it very tightly above. For it is clear that a moderately tight bond can indeed prevent the blood already in the arm from returning to the heart through the veins, but it cannot prevent new blood from always flowing in from the arteries, because they are situated beneath the veins and their walls are harder...

...the skin of these [the arteries] cannot be so easily compressed; and also that the blood coming from the heart strives to pass through them toward the hand with greater force than it can return from there to the heart through the veins. Since this blood leaves the arm through an opening made in one of the veins, there must necessarily be some passages below the bandage—that is, toward the end of the arm—through which it can come from the arteries. He [William Harvey] also excellently proves what he says about the movement of the blood from certain membranes, arranged in various places like valves around the veins, which do not permit blood to pass from the middle of the body to the extremities, but only to return from the extremities to the heart. Furthermore, he proves it by experience, which shows that all the blood in the body can exit in a very short time through a single severed artery, even if it were tied very tightly near the heart and severed between the heart and the ligature; so that there would be no occasion to suspect that the exiting blood comes from anywhere other than the heart.

But there are many other things which testify that what I have said is the true cause of this motion of the blood. First, the difference observed between the blood exiting from the veins and that flowing from the arteries; this can arise from nowhere else than from the fact that by passing through the heart it has been <term>rarefied</term> <note>Descartes believed the heart acted like a furnace where blood expanded (rarefied) and became thinner when heated, rather than the heart acting as a muscular pump.</note> and, as it were, distilled. Thus, it becomes more subtle, vivid, and hot immediately after it exits—that is, when it is contained in the arteries—than it was shortly before entering them, when it was stagnant in the veins. And if one pays close attention, it will be found that this difference only appears clearly in the vicinity of the heart, and less so in places further away from it. Next, the hardness of the coats [walls] of which the **pulmonary artery** <note>original Latin: "vena arteriosa"</note> and the **aorta** <note>original Latin: "magna arteria"</note> are composed shows well enough that the blood beats against them with greater force than against the veins. Why would the left cavity of the heart and the aorta be larger and wider than the right cavity and the pulmonary artery, unless the blood of the pulmonary artery, having only entered the lungs after passing through the heart, were more subtle and rarefied more easily and effectively than the blood coming directly from the **vena cava**? And what can physicians gather from the feeling of the pulse, unless they know that the blood, as it changes its nature, can be rarefied by the heat of the heart more or less, and faster or slower, than before? And if one considers how

<margin>48</margin>
this | heat is communicated to other limbs, must it not be admitted that this happens | by means of the blood, which is heated while passing through the heart and then spreads through the whole body? From this it follows that if blood is removed from any part, heat is removed by the same action. And even if the heart equaled glowing iron in its heat, it would still not suffice to warm the feet and hands as much as we feel, unless it continuously sent new blood there. Furthermore, from this is also recognized the true use of respiration...

...be enough fresh air brought into the lungs to cause the blood—which flows there from the right ventricle of the heart after being <term>rarefied</term> <note>Descartes believed blood expanded into a vapor-like state when heated by the "fire without light" in the heart.</note> and, as it were, changed into vapors—to thicken and be converted back into blood once again before it flows back into the left ventricle. Without this process, the blood would not be fit to fuel the fire that resides there. This is confirmed by the fact that we see that animals lacking lungs have only a single ventricle in the heart; and that in infants, who cannot use their lungs while enclosed in their mothers' wombs, we find an opening <note>original: "foramen quoddam"; referring to what is now called the foramen ovale.</note> through which the blood flows from the <term>vena cava</term> into the left cavity of the heart, and a short tube <note>original: "brevem tubum"; the ductus arteriosus.</note> through which it passes from the pulmonary artery into the great artery <note>The aorta.</note> without traveling through the lungs. 

Next, how would <term>digestion</term> <note>original: "concoctio"; early scientists viewed digestion as a "cooking" process driven by heat.</note> occur in the stomach unless the heart sent heat there through the arteries, together with some of the more fluid parts of the blood which help dissolve the food that has been taken in? Is not the action which converts the juice of this food into blood also easy to understand, if one considers that the blood is distilled by passing through the ventricles of the heart repeatedly, perhaps more than one hundred or two hundred times every single day? 

And what else do we need <margin>49</margin> to explain nutrition and the production of the various <term>humors</term> <note>The different fluids of the body, such as bile or phlegm.</note> in the body, except to say that the force with which the blood, while being rarefied, passes from the heart to the ends of the arteries, causes some of its parts to settle in the limbs where they arrive? There, they take the place of other parts which they push out; and according to the position, the shape, or the smallness of the pores they encounter, some parts flow into certain places rather than others. This is the same way that various types of sieves, simply by being perforated in different ways, serve to separate different types of grain from one another. 

Finally, the thing most deserving of observation here is the generation of the <term>animal spirits</term> <note>For Descartes, these were not "spirits" in a supernatural sense, but the most subtle and active physical particles of the blood.</note>. These are like a very subtle wind, or rather a very pure flame, which, rising continually in great abundance from the heart to the brain, penetrates from there through the nerves into the muscles, and gives movement to all the limbs. There is no need to imagine any other cause to explain why the parts of the blood—which, because they are more agitated and penetrating than the rest, are the most fit to form these spirits—tend toward the brain rather than elsewhere, other than the fact that the arteries carrying them there proceed from the heart in the straightest line of all. According to the rules of mechanics—which are the same as the rules of nature—when several things tend toward the same place at once where there is not enough room for all of them (as is the case for the parts of the blood leaving the left ventricle of the heart and heading for the brain), it is necessary that the weaker and less agitated parts be pushed aside by the stronger ones, which in this way reach their destination alone.

<summary>Descartes explains the mechanical functions of the lungs in cooling blood and the role of the heart's heat in digestion and nutrition. He concludes by describing "animal spirits" as physical particles that travel to the brain to power muscular movement.</summary>

I had explained all these things in detail in the treatise I previously intended to publish <note>Descartes is referring to "The World" (*Le Monde*), which he suppressed after hearing of Galileo's condemnation by the Inquisition.</note>. In that work, I had consequently shown what 
<margin>50</margin> 
the structure of the **nerves** and | **muscles** of the human body must be, to ensure that the **animal spirits** <note>original: "spiritus animales"; Descartes conceived of these not as ghosts, but as a very subtle wind or pure flame that flowed through the hollow tubes of the nerves to move the limbs.</note> contained within them have the power to move its limbs; just as we see that heads, shortly after | they have been severed, still move and bite the earth even though they are no longer animated. I also showed what changes must occur in the brain to produce wakefulness, sleep, and dreams; how light, sounds, smells, tastes, heat, and all other qualities of external objects can imprint various ideas upon it through the organs of the senses; and how hunger, thirst, and other internal affections can also send their own impressions there. I explained what should be understood there as the **common sense** <note>original: "sensum communem"; in early modern psychology, this was a specific faculty in the brain that unified the data from all five senses.</note>, in which these ideas are received; by the memory, which preserves them; and by the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasiam".</note>, which can change them in various ways and compose new ones; and which, by also distributing the animal spirits in various ways into the muscles, can cause the limbs of that body to move in the same way as we respond to external objects striking our sense organs, or to our internal affections—matching all those movements that occur in us without the command of the will. This will not seem strange at all to those who know how many different movements can be produced by **automata** <note>original: "automatis"; self-moving machines like clockwork figures, which were popular in the gardens of the wealthy during this era.</note> built by human industry, | and this with the help of only a few wheels and other instruments, when compared with the almost infinite multitude of bones, muscles, nerves, arteries, veins, and other organic parts found in the body of any animal. They will consider the mechanism of the human body as an automaton made by the hands of God, which is infinitely better ordered and possesses in
<margin>51</margin>
itself movements more | admirable than any that can be manufactured by human art.

And here I had dwelled particularly on showing that, if there were such machines that possessed the external shape and all the organs of an ape or any other irrational animal, we would have no way to recognize that they differed in their nature from those animals. However, if there were any that bore the image of our bodies and imitated our actions as far as was morally possible, we would always have two very certain ways to recognize that they were not, for that reason, true humans. The first is that they would never have the use of **speech** <note>original: "sermonis".</note>, or of any signs, such as we use to open our thoughts to others. For one can indeed conceive of a machine so constructed that it utters some words—even that it speaks some things in response to the presence of external objects that move its organs,

...respond appropriately: as if it were touched in one place, it might ask what we want from it; if in another, it might cry out that we are hurting it, and other such things; but not so that it could arrange its words of its own accord to | respond appropriately to everything said in its presence; as even the dullest of men can do. The second is that even if such machines did many things as well as, or perhaps better than any of us, they would undoubtedly fail in others; by which one could recognize that they do not act by reason, but only from the arrangement of their organs. For while reason is a universal instrument <note>original: "ratio instrumentum sit universale"; Descartes argues that reason is a single, flexible faculty that applies to all situations, unlike mechanical parts which are specialized for only one task.</note> that can serve in every kind of situation, these organs, on the other hand, require a specific arrangement for each particular action. Hence it is clearly incredible that there should be enough different organs in any machine | to respond to all the external movements 
<margin>52</margin>

For it is noteworthy that there are no men so dull and stupid, not even excluding the insane <note>original: "amentibus"; literally those "without mind."</note>, that they cannot arrange different words together and compose a speech from them by which they make their thoughts known; whereas, on the contrary, there is no other animal, however perfect or well-born it may be <note>original: "felici sidere natum"; literally "born under a lucky star," meaning naturally gifted.</note>, that does anything similar. And this does not happen because of a lack of organs; for we see that magpies and parrots <note>original: "picas & psittacos"</note> can utter the same words as we do, and yet cannot speak as we do—that is, in a way that shows they understand what they are saying. Nevertheless, men who are deaf and mute from birth, and who are thus deprived of the organs others use | for speaking—as much as, or even more than beasts—usually invent for themselves, by their own ingenuity, certain signs by which they reveal their minds to those they live with, and who have the leisure to learn their language. This indicates not only that beasts have less power of reason than humans, but that they are entirely devoid of reason. For we see that very little reason is required for speaking; and because some inequality of talent is observed among animals of the same species, no less than among humans, and some are more capable of instruction than others; it is incredible that a monkey or a parrot, the most perfect of its species, should not be able to equal the most stupid child, or at least one with a disordered mind, unless their souls were of a nature entirely different from our own. And it must be noted that speech <note>original: "loquelam"</note> and all the signs | which, by human convention, signify thoughts, 
<margin>53</margin> 
differ greatly from the natural cries and signs that indicate bodily affections. Nor should we think, as some of the ancients did, that beasts speak, but that we [do not understand their language...] <note>The sentence is interrupted at the end of the page; "ser-" likely refers to "sermonem" or speech.</note>

### ON METHOD
<meta>58-60.</meta>

[...they] do not understand speech. For if that were true, since they are provided with many organs analogous to our own, they would be able to make their minds as known to us as they do to their own kind. It is also worthy of special notice that although there are many animals that show more industry <note>original: "industriae"; here Descartes refers to specialized skill or mechanical efficiency.</note> than we do in certain of their actions, those same animals are seen to demonstrate none at all in many others. Thus, the fact that they do things better than we do does not prove that they are endowed with reason; for if it did, it would follow that they possessed a greater reason than any of us, and that they should surpass us in every other thing as well. | Rather, it proves that they are devoid of reason, and that nature acts in them according to the arrangement of their organs: just as we see that a clock, composed only of wheels and weights, can count the hours and measure time more accurately than we can with all our wisdom.

Afterward, I described the rational soul <term>rational soul (anima rationalis): for Descartes, this is the unique, non-material component of human beings that allows for thought and language, distinguishing them from the "animal-machines."</term>, and I showed that it can in no way be drawn from the power of matter, like the other things I had discussed, but that it must be specifically created. Nor is it enough for the soul to reside in the body like a sailor in a ship <note>original: "instar nautae in navi"; a classic philosophical metaphor used to describe a soul that is merely driving a body rather than being unified with it.</note>, except perhaps to move its limbs; rather, it is required that it be more closely joined and united with the body, in order to have senses and appetites similar to ours, and thus to compose a true human being. Furthermore, I have been a little more detailed here in treating the argument concerning the soul because it is of the greatest importance. <margin>54</margin> For after the error of those who deny God—which I believe I have | sufficiently refuted above—there is none that more easily turns weak souls from the straight path of virtue than the idea that the soul of beasts is of the same nature as our own; and that, consequently, we have nothing to fear or hope for after this life, any more than flies or ants. But when one rightly recognizes how much they differ, the reasons proving that our soul is of a nature entirely independent of the body are much better understood; and consequently, that it is not bound to die with it. Finally, because | no causes are observed that might destroy it, we are naturally led to judge that the soul is immortal.

<margin>VI. What the Author thinks is required to progress further in the investigation of Nature than has been done so far; and the reasons that compelled him to write.</margin>

Three years have now passed since I reached the end of the treatise containing all these matters, and I was beginning to revise it so that I might hand it over to the printer; however, I learned that men to whom I defer greatly, and whose authority has no less power over my actions than my own reason has over my thoughts, had disapproved of a certain opinion in Physics <note>Descartes is referring to the condemnation of Galileo Galilei by the Roman Inquisition in 1633 for advocating that the Earth revolves around the sun.</note> published shortly before by someone else. I do not wish to say that I adhered to that opinion, but only that I had observed nothing in it, prior to their censure, that I could suspect to be harmful to either religion or the state; and therefore, nothing that would have prevented me from defending it, if reason...

<meta>60-62.</meta>

[...someone else] had persuaded me was true; and this struck me with the fear that among my own opinions, one might be found in which I had strayed from the truth—even though I have always taken great care not to give credit to any new opinions for which I did not have the most certain demonstrations, nor to write anything that could result in harm to anyone. However, this was sufficient to move me to abandon my plan of publishing them.

<margin>55</margin>
For even if the reasons that had induced me to publish my thoughts were very strong, my own temperament <note>original: "genius"; here meaning his natural disposition or character.</note>, which has always abhorred the writing of books, caused me immediately to find many other reasons to excuse myself from undertaking that labor. These reasons on both sides are such that it is not only somewhat in my interest to recount them here, but perhaps also in the interest of the "Republic of Letters" <note>The international community of intellectuals and scholars who shared ideas across borders in the 17th century.</note> to know them.

I never made much of the things that proceeded from my own mind; and as long as I gathered no other fruits from the Method I use, except that I satisfied myself regarding certain doubts belonging to the speculative sciences, or attempted to order my own conduct <note>original: "mores"; refers to ethics and personal behavior.</note> according to the reasons it taught me, I did not think myself bound to write anything on the matter. For as far as conduct is concerned, everyone is so full of their own sense that one could find as many reformers as there are heads, if it were permitted for anyone—other than those whom God has established as the supreme rulers of their peoples, or those whom He has gifted with a large enough measure of grace and zeal to be prophets—to undertake to change anything therein. And although my speculations pleased me very much, I believed that others also had their own, which perhaps pleased them even more. But as soon as I had acquired some general notions concerning Physics, and beginning to test them in various particular difficulties, I observed how far they could lead me, and how much they differ from the principles that have been in use until now; I believed I could not keep them hidden without a grave sin against the law which commands us to procure, as much as is in us, the general good of all mankind.

<margin>56</margin>
For through them, I realized that it is possible to arrive at knowledge that is very useful for life; and that in place of that speculative Philosophy taught in the **Schools** <term>Schools (Scholae): refers to Scholasticism, the traditional academic philosophy of the Middle Ages and Renaissance, which Descartes viewed as overly abstract and impractical.</term>, a **Practical philosophy** can be found. By knowing the power and actions of fire, water, air, the stars, the heavens, and all the other bodies that surround us, as distinctly as we know the various crafts of our artisans, we could likewise apply them to all the uses for which they are fit, and thus make ourselves as it were the **masters and possessors of nature**. This is surely to be desired, not only for the invention of an infinity of devices that would allow us to enjoy the fruits of the earth and all its comforts without any labor, but especially also for health...

### ON METHOD
<meta>62-64.</meta>

...the preservation of health, which is undoubtedly the first good of this life and the foundation of all others. For the mind <note>original: "animus"; referring to the soul or intellect in its relation to the body.</note> depends so much on the temperament <note>In 17th-century science, "temperament" referred to the specific balance of bodily humors or qualities that determined a person's health and character.</note> and the arrangement of the body's organs that, if it is possible to find some means that makes men wiser and more ingenious than they have been until now, I believe it must be sought in **Medicine**. 

It is true that the medicine currently in use contains few things of such remarkable utility. But though I have no intention of despising it, I am confident there is no one—even among those who practice it as a profession—who would not admit that everything discovered in it so far is almost nothing compared to what remains to be known. We could be free from an infinite number of diseases, both of body and mind, and perhaps even from the weakening effects of old age, if we had sufficient knowledge of the causes from which these evils arise and of all the remedies with which nature has provided us. 

Since I have resolved to spend my whole life in the pursuit of such a necessary science, and have happened upon a path which seems to me such that, if one follows it, they will undoubtedly reach the desired <margin>57</margin> end—unless hindered by the brevity of life or a lack of experiments <note>original: "experimentorum"; in this period, the term "experiment" often referred to both structured tests and general observations or experiences.</note>—I judged there was no better remedy against these two obstacles than to faithfully communicate to the public everything I had found, however small it might be. I wished to urge great minds to strive to go further, each contributing according to their ability to the performing of experiments, and also to share with the public everything they might learn. In this way, the last might begin where their predecessors left off, and by thus combining the lives and labors of many, we might all together progress much further than any individual could privately.

Moreover, concerning experiences, I observed that they become more necessary the more knowledge one has acquired. In the beginning, it is better to use only those which present themselves spontaneously to our senses and which we cannot be ignorant of if we pay them even the slightest attention, rather than to search for more rare and abstruse ones. The reason for this is that these rarer experiences often deceive us as long as the causes of more common ones remain unknown; the circumstances on which they depend are almost always so particular and minute that they are very difficult to observe. 

However, I have followed this order: First, I tried to find in general the **principles** or first causes of everything that exists or can exist in the world, by looking to God alone who created it, and deriving them from no other source than certain seeds of truth naturally implanted in our souls. Afterward, I examined what were the first and most ordinary effects that could be deduced from these causes; and it seems to me...

### ON METHOD

...by this path, I have come to know the heavens, the stars, the earth, and even on the earth,
<margin>58</margin>
water, air, fire, minerals, and other such things which are the most common and simple of all, and therefore the easiest to understand. Then, when I wished to descend to more particular things, so many diverse objects presented themselves to me that I believed it would require a genius more than human to distinguish the forms or species of bodies <note>original: "formas aut species corporum"; in the philosophy of the time, "forms" were the internal principles that gave things their specific characteristics.</note> that are on the earth from the infinite others that *could* be there, if it had pleased God to place them there. I believed it impossible to distinguish them and then apply them to our use, unless we meet causes through their effects <note>This is a classic description of "a posteriori" reasoning—working backward from the observed result to the underlying cause.</note> and are aided by many particular experiments <note>original: "experimentis"; in the 17th century, this term covered both casual observations and structured scientific tests.</note>. Then, reflecting in my mind upon all the objects that had ever presented themselves to my senses, I will not be afraid to say that I have observed nothing in them which I could not explain quite conveniently through the principles I had found. 

But I must also confess that the power of Nature is so broad and vast, and these principles are so simple and general, that I observe hardly any particular effect anymore which I do not immediately recognize as being deducible from those principles in various ways; and usually, nothing seems more difficult to me than to find in which of these ways the effect depends upon them. For I cannot extricate myself from this difficulty in any other way than by seeking new experiments, which are such that their result would not be the same if the effect is explained in one way as it would be if explained in another. Furthermore, I have now reached a point where I think I see clearly enough how most of the experiments that can serve this purpose ought to be conducted. But I also see that they are such, and so numerous, that neither my hands nor my resources, even if they were a thousand times greater, could suffice for them all. Consequently, according to the opportunity I shall have from now on to conduct more or fewer of them, I promise myself more or less progress in the knowledge of Nature.

<margin>59</margin>
This is what I hoped to declare in the treatise I had composed <note>He is referring to his work *The World* (*Le Monde*), which he famously decided not to publish after the condemnation of Galileo in 1633.</note>, and to reveal there so clearly the utility that the public would gain from it, that I might induce all those who have the common good of humanity at heart—that is, all who are truly honorable men and not merely in appearance—both to communicate to me the experiments they had already made, and to help me in the investigation of those that remain to be done.

But since that time, other reasons have occurred to me which have led me to change my mind, and to think that I ought indeed to continue writing down all the things I consider to be of any importance as soon as I discover their truth; and to do so with no less care than if I intended to publish them. I do this partly so that I may have all the better opportunity to examine them well—for without doubt, that which is intended to be read by many is always more accurately laboured over...

### ON METHOD.

...is more believable than what is written only for private use; and often what seemed true to me when I first conceived it, I later realized was false when I tried to commit it to paper. At the same time, I did not want to lose any opportunity to provide for the public utility as much as I could. If my writings were of any value, those into whose hands they might fall after my death could use them as they see fit. But I felt I should by no means permit them to be published while I lived, lest the oppositions and controversies with which they might perhaps be harassed, or even whatever fame they might gain, should give me any occasion to lose the time I had designated for my research <note>original: "institutioni meæ"; referring to his foundational scientific and philosophical plan.</note>. For even though it is true that every person is bound,

<margin>60</margin>

as much as they can, to provide for the good of others, and that someone who is useful to nobody is worth nothing, it is also true that our concerns should extend beyond the present time. It is good to omit things that might bring some utility to the living, with the goal of doing other things that will be much more beneficial to our descendants. Just as I do not wish to hide that the little I have learned so far is almost nothing compared to what I do not know, and which I do not despair of reaching the knowledge of. For it is almost the same with those who gradually uncover truth in the sciences as it is with those who grow rich: it is easier for them to make large gains than it was before to make much smaller ones when they were still poor. Or they can be compared with generals of armies, whose forces tend to increase in proportion to their victories, and who, after a defeat, need more prudence to preserve their remaining troops than they needed when they were superior in battle to occupy cities and provinces. For truly, he settles a battle <note>Descartes uses the metaphor of "deciding a battle" to describe the act of resolving a major intellectual problem.</note> who tries to overcome all the difficulties and errors that prevent him from reaching the knowledge of truth; and he is defeated in battle who admits a false opinion on a matter of some importance. He then needs more dexterity to restore himself to his former state than to make great progress when he already has certain principles. As for me, if I have found any truths in the sciences (and I trust that what is contained in this volume will show that I have found some), I can say they are only the consequences of five or six principal difficulties I have overcome, which I count as so many battles in which I have won the victory. Indeed, I will not fear to say that I think

<margin>61</margin>

nothing more is lacking for me to reach my goal than to win two or three more such battles; and I am not so advanced in age that, according to the ordinary course of nature, I might not have enough leisure left for this task. But I believe I am all the more bound [to manage my] time—

<page-num>578</page-num>
<header>WORKS OF DESCARTES. 68-69.</header>

the little time that remains to me is so scarce, I have all the more hope of using it well. I would undoubtedly have many opportunities to lose that time if I published the foundations of my **Physics** <term>Physics: In Descartes' time, this referred to the general study of nature and the physical world, not just the specific modern discipline.</term>. For even though almost everything in them is so evident that one only needs to understand them to agree, and there is nothing among them for which I do not hope to provide demonstrations; nevertheless, because it is impossible for them to agree with the many diverse opinions of others, I foresee that I would frequently be distracted from my purpose by the opposition they would provoke.

It could indeed be objected that these oppositions would be useful, both to help me recognize my errors and so that, if I have found anything good, others might gain a greater understanding of it through this process; and because many eyes see more than one, those who now begin to use my findings might, in turn, help me with their own discoveries. But although I recognize that I am very prone to error, and I almost never trust the first thoughts that occur to me, the experience I have with the objections that can be made against me prevents me from hoping for any benefit from them. For I have already often experienced the judgments of those I considered friends, as well as others I thought were indifferent to me, and even some malicious and envious people whom I knew would try to drag into the open what the veil of friendship hid from the eyes of friends. But it has rarely happened that anything was objected to me that I had not in some way foreseen, unless it was | <margin>62</margin> || remote from my argument; so much so that I have almost never encountered a critic of my opinions who did not seem to me either less rigorous or less fair than I am to myself. Likewise, I have never observed that any previously unknown truth was brought to light through the help of Scholastic <term>Scholastic: Referring to the traditional university system of the Middle Ages and Renaissance, which relied heavily on debating established texts like those of Aristotle.</term> disputes. For while everyone strives to win, people usually pay more attention to probability <note>original: "verisimilitudinem," meaning a likeness to truth or plausibility rather than absolute truth.</note> than to the weight of the arguments brought forward on both sides; and those who have been good advocates for a long time are not necessarily better judges afterward.

As for the benefit that others might receive from the communication of my **Meditations** <note>original: "meditationum"; here referring to his philosophical reflections on the nature of reality.</note>, it could not be very great yet, because I have not yet brought them to the point where nothing remains to be added before they are put into practice. And I think I can say without boasting that if anyone is capable of completing them, it is I rather than anyone else. Not because there may not be minds in the world that surpass mine by many leagues <term>parafangs: Originally an ancient Persian measure of distance (approx. 3.5 miles); Descartes uses it here metaphorically to mean "by a vast distance."</term>; but because it is impossible to conceive a thing so well and make it one's own when learning it from another as when one finds it for oneself. This is so true in this matter that although I have often explained some of my opinions to men...

<summary>Descartes argues that publishing his work prematurely would invite distractions and useless academic debates, which rarely lead to truth. He asserts that the original inventor of an idea is better suited to perfect it than those who learn it second-hand.</summary>

<page-num>579</page-num>

### ON METHOD.

<meta>Top left: 69-71.</meta>

...even the most acute minds, and those who seemed to understand my ideas very clearly while I was speaking; nevertheless, when they repeated them, I observed that they almost always changed them so much that I could no longer recognize them as my own. On this occasion, I wish to ask posterity here never to believe that anything has come from me which I myself have not published. And I am in no way surprised by those absurd dogmas <term>Dogmas: Established beliefs or doctrines held to be authoritatively true.</term> attributed to those ancient philosophers whose writings we do not possess; nor do I judge because of this that their 
<margin>63</margin> thoughts were very far from reason, since they possessed the most excellent minds of their centuries; but rather that these thoughts were reported to us incorrectly. Just as we also see, it has almost never happened that they were surpassed by any of their followers. And I believe the most fervent of those who now follow Aristotle <note>original: "Aristotelem"</note> would consider themselves blessed if they equaled him in the knowledge of nature; even on the condition that they would learn nothing more thereafter. 

In this they are like ivy, which never strives to climb higher than the trees that support it; indeed, it often grows downward after it has reached the very top. For it seems to me that those people also descend—that is, in some way make themselves more unlearned than if they had desisted from their studies—who, not content with knowing all those things which are clearly and lucidly explained in their Author, wish besides to find there the solution to many difficulties of which he makes not even a word of mention, and perhaps never even thought of. 

Nevertheless, their way of philosophizing is very convenient for minds positioned below mediocrity. For the obscurity of the distinctions and principles they use is the reason they can speak as confidently about everything as if they knew them perfectly; and thus they can defend everything they say against the most subtle and acute minds, so that they cannot be proven wrong. In this matter they seem to me like a blind man who, in order to fight on equal terms against a sighted person, had led him into some deep and dark cellar. And I can say it is in their interest that I abstain from publishing the principles of the Philosophy I use. For since they are most simple and evident, I would be doing almost the same thing, by giving them light, as if I were to open some windows through which light would enter 
<margin>64</margin> into that cellar where they have descended to fight. 

Indeed, even more excellent minds have no reason to desire to know these principles. For if they wish to know how to speak about everything and to acquire a reputation for erudition <term>Erudition: Extensive knowledge acquired chiefly from books; profound scholarly learning.</term>, they will achieve this more easily if they are content with probability <note>original: "verisimilitudine" — literally 'likeness to truth.' Descartes refers to plausible but unproven arguments favored by scholastics.</note>, which can be found without great labor in every kind of matter, than by investigating the truth, which reveals itself only gradually in certain things, and which, when one must speak of other things, forces a frank confession of one's ignorance. If, however, they prefer the knowledge of a few truths to the vain profession of being ignorant of nothing—as it is undoubtedly to be preferred—and my...

### WORKS OF DESCARTES.

<meta>71-73.</meta>

...who wish to follow this undertaking <note>original: "institutum"</note> have no need for me to say anything more to them than what they have already heard from me in this dissertation. For if they are capable of advancing further than I have done, they will be much more able to find by themselves everything that I think I have found so far; since I have never examined anything except in order, it is certain that what remains for me to bring out of the darkness | is much more difficult and hidden in itself than what I was able to find before; and they would have much less pleasure in learning it from me than from themselves. Besides, the habit <term>Habitus: A settled or regular tendency or practice, especially one that is hard to give up; here, a mental discipline.</term> which they will acquire for themselves—by seeking easy things first, and passing little by little and by degrees to other more difficult ones—will be more useful to them than all my instructions. Just as for my part, if I had been taught from my youth all the truths whose demonstrations I later investigated, and if I had learned them without labor, I think perhaps I would never have known many more; at least I would never have acquired the habit and ease with which I hope to always find new ones, as I apply my mind to investigating them. And, to put it in a word, if there is any work in the world that cannot be completed so well by | another as by the one who began it, it is this one in which I am engaged and labor. <margin>65</margin>

It is true indeed that, as far as the experiments <note>original: "experimenta"; in this context, it refers to both scientific experiments and general experiences or observations.</note> are concerned which can serve this goal, one man is not equal to performing them all. But he could also use no other hands usefully than his own, except perhaps those of craftsmen, or other such hired workers, whom the hope of gain (a very effective means) would drive to do accurately everything he prescribed to them. For as for volunteers, who, moved by curiosity or a desire to learn, might perhaps offer their help to him of their own accord, besides the fact that they ordinarily promise much and perform little, and almost none of their projects ever reach the desired end; | they would without doubt want their labor compensated by the explanation of certain difficulties, or at least by useless social courtesies and conversations, in which he could not spend a part of his leisure without great loss. And as for experiments already done by others, even if they were willing to share them with him—which those who hold them as secrets will never do—they are usually accompanied by so many circumstances and superfluous things that it would be very difficult for him to extract the truth from them. Besides, he would find almost everything so poorly explained, or even false (because those who did them wanted to see in them only what they thought conformed to their principles), that if some were suited to his purpose, they could still not equal the value of the time that would have to be spent in selecting them. So much so that if there were someone in this world whom...

<page-num>581</page-num>

### 73-75. ON METHOD.

<margin>66</margin>If it were well known that there was someone capable of discovering the greatest things and those most useful for the public, and for that reason other men strove in every way to assist him in achieving his purpose, I do not see how they could do anything else for his sake except contribute to the expenses of the experiments <note>original: "experimenta"; here referring to both scientific trials and observations</note> he might need, and otherwise prevent his time from being stolen by the unwanted interruptions <note>original: "importunitate"</note> of anyone. But I do not attribute so much to myself that I would wish to promise anything extraordinary, nor do I feed myself with such vain thoughts as to think that the public <note>original: "rempublicam"; here meaning society or the common good</note> ought to care much about my plans; nor am I of such a lowly spirit that I would want to accept a benefit from anyone that I might be believed unworthy of receiving.

All these considerations joined together have been the reason why, for three years, I have been unwilling to publish the treatise <note>Descartes is referring to "The World" (Le Monde), a work he suppressed after learning of the condemnation of Galileo in 1633.</note> which I had in hand—and even why I resolved not to make any other work public during my lifetime that was so general, or from which the foundations of my physics could be understood. But since then, there have been two other reasons that moved me to add certain particular specimens <note>These "specimens" were the Dioptrics, the Meteors, and the Geometry, which were published alongside the Discourse on Method.</note> here, and to give the public some account of my actions and plans. The first of these is that if I omitted to do so, many who knew of my previous intention to submit certain writings to the press might suspect that the reasons for which I abstained were less honorable to me than they truly are. For although I do not excessively desire glory—or even, if I may say so, I shrink from it, insofar as I judge it contrary to that tranquility which I value above all things—I have nonetheless never sought to hide my actions as if they were crimes, nor have I taken many precautions to remain unknown. This is partly because I would have believed this an injustice against myself, and partly because it would have caused me a certain restlessness, which again would have been contrary to the perfect peace of mind I was seeking.

<margin>67</margin>And because, while I remained indifferent to the choice of being known or remaining hidden, I could not prevent myself from gaining some degree of reputation, I thought I should at least do my best to avoid having a bad one.

The other reason that compelled me to write this is that I see, more and more every day, the delay suffered by my plan to instruct myself, because of the infinite experiments I need and which I cannot perform without the help of others. Although I am not so much of a *Suffenus* <term>Suffenus: A reference to a character from the poet Catullus, used here to mean a person who is self-satisfied or has an inflated sense of their own talent.</term> that I hope the public will wish to take a great interest in my affairs, I nevertheless do not wish to be so lacking in my duty to myself that I give those who come after me a reason to one day reproach me, saying that I could have left them many things much better than I did, if I had not too much neglected to signify to them how they could promote my designs.

<summary>Descartes explains that while he values his privacy and tranquility above fame, he is publishing these "specimens" of his work to avoid a bad reputation and to ensure future generations cannot blame him for failing to ask for the assistance necessary to complete his scientific experiments.</summary>
<keywords>Descartes, Method, experiments, physics, tranquility, Suffenus, public utility, reputation, scientific collaboration</keywords>

<page-num>582, 75-77.</page-num>
# WORKS OF DESCARTES

<margin>68</margin>
And I thought it would be easy for me to select certain subjects that would not be subject to much controversy, nor would they force me to explain more of my principles than I desire; yet they would still clearly enough reveal what I can or cannot achieve in the sciences. Whether I have succeeded in this, I leave for others to judge; but it will be very pleasing to me if these works are examined. To provide a greater opportunity for this, I ask all those who wish to raise any objections against them to send these to my bookseller <note>original: "bibliopolam"; Descartes refers to his publisher, Jean Maire of Leiden.</note>. Once notified by him, I will attempt to append my response at the same time; in this way, readers seeing both writings together will be able to judge the truth all the more easily. I do not promise to offer long responses, but only to candidly confess my errors if I recognize them, or, if I cannot perceive them, simply to say what I think is required for the defense of what I have written. I will not add an explanation of any new material, so that I am not forced to move endlessly from one subject to another.

<margin>69</margin>
But if some of the things I discussed at the beginning of the *Dioptrics* <note>original: "Dioptrices"; his treatise on light and optics.</note> and the *Meteors* <note>original: "Meteorum"; his treatise on atmospheric phenomena and rainbows.</note> should be offensive at first glance because I call them "hypotheses" and seem unwilling to prove them, I ask that the entire treatises be read with attention, and I hope that those who hesitate will find satisfaction. For the reasons in them seem to me to be connected in such a sequence that, just as the last things are demonstrated by the first (which are their causes), so reciprocally the first are proved by the last (which are their effects). Nor should anyone think that I fall here into the error that logicians call a "Circle" <note>original: "Logici Circulum"; referring to the logical fallacy of circular reasoning, or *petitio principii*.</note>. For since experience shows the greatest part of these effects to be most certain, the causes from which I derive them serve not so much to prove them as to explain them; and on the contrary, the causes themselves are proved by the effects. I have called them "hypotheses" for no other purpose than to make it known that I am confident I can deduce them from those first truths which I explained above; but I have deliberately chosen not to do so, to prevent certain minds—who think they can learn in a single day what someone else has struggled with for twenty years, as soon as he has revealed it to them in only a word or two (and who are more prone to error and less capable of perceiving truth the more clever and quick they are)—from taking the opportunity to build some absurd philosophy upon those principles which they will take for mine, and the blame for this being attributed to me. For as far as the opinions that are entirely mine are concerned, I do not wish to excuse their novelty; since if the reasons upon which they rest are well weighed, I am confident they will be found so simple and so in conformity with common sense <note>original: "sensui communi"</note> that they will seem less extraordinary and paradoxical than any others that can be held on the same subjects. Nor do I boast of being the first inventor of any of them, but only that I have never adopted them as my own—

<summary>Descartes invites public criticism through his publisher and explains his "reciprocal" method of proof, where causes explain effects and effects confirm causes. He defends his use of hypotheses as a way to prevent superficial thinkers from misusing his foundational principles to create "absurd" philosophies.</summary>

->### ON THE METHOD###<-
<meta>Ref: 77-78.</meta>

...[accepted] these things, either because they had been previously received by others, or because they had not been; but for this sole reason: that **reason** <note>original: "ratio"; the fundamental human capacity for logic and discernment.</note> itself had persuaded me of them.

If craftsmen <note>original: "artifices"; referring here to lens-grinders and instrument makers.</note> cannot so quickly put into execution the invention explained in the *Dioptrics*, I do not believe it can be rightly blamed for that reason. For great skill and practice are needed to build the machines I described, and to adapt them so that no detail is missing; nor would I be less surprised if they succeeded on their first attempt than if someone were able to learn to play the lute <note>original: "testudine"; literally "tortoise shell," a classical term for the lute or lyre.</note> excellently in a single day, simply because the best method of playing had been described to him.

<margin>70</margin>
For the rest, I do not wish to say anything specific here about the progress I hope to make in the sciences hereafter, or to bind myself to the public with any promise that I am uncertain whether I can fulfill or not. But I will only say that I have decided to devote the remainder of my life to no other thing than to acquiring such knowledge of nature from which more certain rules for **Medicine** <note>Descartes viewed the improvement of health and the extension of life as the primary practical goal of his philosophy.</note> than have existed until now can be derived; and my nature is so averse to every other kind of purpose—especially those which cannot benefit some without harming others—that if I were driven by some occasion to pursue such things, I do not believe I could achieve anything distinguished in them. I openly profess this here, even though I am not unaware that this profession is useless for acquiring any authority or reputation; which indeed I so little desire, that I shall always consider myself more indebted to those by whose favor I may enjoy my **leisure** <note>original: "otio"; scholarly peace or freedom from public business.</note> without hindrance, than to those who might offer me the highest honors.

<header>DIOPTRICS <note>original: "Dioptrice"; the branch of optics dealing with the refraction of light, especially through lenses.</note></header>

# CHAPTER ONE.

->On Light.<-

<margin>71</margin>
1. The conduct of our entire life depends upon our senses, among which sight is the noblest and most far-reaching; thus, there is no doubt that those inventions which can increase its power are most useful. It is certainly difficult to imagine any invention that helps more than those wonderful glasses <note>original: "specilla"; a term used in the 17th century for telescopes or magnifying lenses.</note> which, in the short time since they became known, have already detected new stars in the heavens and other new bodies on the earth, more numerous than those seen before. Indeed, by extending the sharp edge of our vision beyond the limits where the imagination of our ancestors was stopped, they seem to have opened a path for us to a greater and more absolute knowledge of nature. But we owe this invention—so useful and wonderful—not to the credit of our sciences, but rather to wandering experiments and a stroke of chance, much to the shame of our knowledge. About thirty years ago, there lived a certain Jacob Metius <note>Jacob Metius (c. 1571–1628) was a Dutch instrument-maker; he is one of several men credited with the invention of the telescope.</note>, born in Alkmaar <note>original: "Alcmariæ"; a city in the Netherlands.</note>, a city in Holland. He was a man completely unskilled in the liberal arts, although he had a father and a brother who were practitioners of Mathematics. His greatest pleasure was to shape mirrors and burning glasses <term>vitra ustoria: lenses designed to concentrate sunlight to create heat or fire</term>, even making some from ice during the winter—a material which, as experience shows, is not entirely unsuited for that purpose. Since he had many glasses of various shapes on hand for this reason, by a fortunate fate he happened to look through two of them at once: <margin>72</margin> one of which was slightly thicker in the middle than at the edges, while the other was, vice versa, much thicker at the edges than in the middle. He applied them so successfully to the two ends of a tube that the first telescope <note>original: "telescopium".</note> of the kind we are discussing was created. And it is according to the standard of this single model that all those we have had up to this day have been crafted; nor has there yet appeared anyone, as far as I know, who has sufficiently demonstrated what specific shape these glasses require. Although many brilliant minds have since emerged who have cultivated this field quite a lot, and have on that occasion discovered various things in optics <note>original: "Opticis".</note> more excellent than those we inherited from our ancestors,

<page-num>585</page-num>
<header>DIOPTRICS <note>original: "Dioptrice"; the study of the refraction of light through lenses.</note></header>

However, since more complex inventions rarely reach their highest degree of perfection at the very moment they are born, quite a few difficulties have been left here to provide me with material for writing. And since the construction of these things I shall discuss depends upon the skill and industry of craftsmen—who for the most part have no leisure for scholarly letters—I will endeavor to ensure | that anyone can easily grasp what I say. I shall withhold nothing, nor shall I assume anything that must be sought from any other discipline. Therefore, I will begin with an explanation of light and its rays; afterward, having briefly described the parts of the eye, I will accurately explain the manner in which vision occurs; and finally, having noted all those things that one might wish for to perfect it, I will teach by what artifices those very things can be provided.

2. Here, however, I have no other reason to speak of light or brightness <note>original: "de luce, vel lumine"; Latin distinguishes between the source of light (lux) and the light that fills a space (lumen).</note> than to explain how its rays enter the eyes and can be bent by the encounter of various bodies. Thus, it will not be necessary to inquire into what its true nature is; instead, I will offer two or three comparisons here, which I believe are sufficient to help conceive of light in the way that is most convenient of all for explaining its 
<margin>73</margin> properties—which experience has already taught—and consequently for discovering all others that are not so easily noticed through use. This is much like in Astronomy, where from hypotheses that may even be false or uncertain, provided they agree accurately with all that is observed in the heavens, many very true and certain conclusions are usually deduced regarding things that have not been observed.

There is none of us who has not happened at some time, while walking at night without a torch through rough and obstructed places, to have used a staff to guide his steps; and then we were able to notice | that through the intermediary of the staff, we felt the various bodies encountered all around us; likewise, we could distinguish whether there was a tree, or a stone, or sand, or water, or grass, or mud, or some such thing. It must be admitted that this kind of sensing is obscure and quite confused in those who have not been taught by long practice; but let us consider it in those who, having been born blind, have had to use it for their entire lives. We will find it so perfect and complete that we might say they see, in a way, with their hands, or that the staff <term>scipio<gloss>a staff or walking stick</gloss></term> is given to them as the organ of some sixth sense, provided to supply the defect of their sight.

3. Now, therefore, to establish a comparison, let us imagine light in a luminous body to be nothing other than a certain motion, or a prompt and vivid action, which proceeds through the air and other interjected transparent bodies toward the eyes, in exactly the same way that the motion or resistance of the bodies which this blind man encounters travels to his hand through the interposed staff. And immediately from this, cease to wonder—
